candidates.title: Towards automatically identifying contingent responses: differentiating toddlers based on human-robot interactions
candidates.abstract: This study characterizes baseline patterns of proxemic behavior in typically developing toddlers during a structured interaction with a social robot. Using overhead video and a convolutional neural network, we automatically identified the locations of the child, robot, and other individuals in the room and extracted distance-based measures throughout the interaction. These behavioral measures were analyzed alongside standardized developmental assessment scores to quantify variability within this normative sample. The combined data demonstrated substantial variability in children's proxemic behaviors, highlighting the range of ways young children engage with a novel robotic partner. These findings provide foundational descriptive data for early-childhood human-robot interaction and establish a methodological framework that future hypothesis-driven studies, including those involving clinically diagnosed populations, can build upon. No diagnostic or screening interpretations should be drawn from this work.

candidates.title: Stakeholder Perspectives on Whether and How Social Robots Can Support Self-Advocacy for Higher Education Students with Disabilities
candidates.abstract: This article presents an iterative, participatory, empirical study that examines the potential of using artificial intelligence, such as social robots and large language models, to support mediation and advocacy for disabled students in higher education. Drawing on qualitative data from interviews and focus groups conducted with various stakeholders, including disabled students, disabled student representatives and disability practitioners at the University of Cambridge, this study reports findings relating to understanding the problem space, ideating robotic support and participatory co-design of advocacy support robots. The findings position these technologies as student-controlled interfaces for navigating disability support, e.g., providing signposting, self-advocacy rehearsal and study companionship, rather than as empathic substitutes for human support, while also surfacing limitations around empathic understanding, trust, equity and accessibility. We discuss ethical considerations, including intersectional biases, the double empathy problem and the implications of deploying social robots in contexts shaped by structural inequalities. Finally, we offer a concrete design framework that distils key considerations for disabled students potentially relevant to comparable HE contexts as well as a broader set of ethical design guidelines that rethink the notion of corrective technological interventions to tools that empower and amplify self-advocacy.

candidates.title: A Taxonomy of Mental Model Mismatches for Human–Robot Interaction
candidates.abstract: Mental model mismatches (MMM) in human–robot interaction occur when humans’ internal representations of robots diverge from robots’ actual properties or behaviors, leading to communication breakdowns, task failures, and reduced trust. These mismatches are subtle and difficult to detect, yet the field lacks shared terminology to identify specific types. This makes it difficult to diagnose problems, design targeted interventions, or compare findings across studies. We present a theoretically grounded taxonomy of 16 MMM types organized by the Sense–Plan–Act (SPA) architecture into sensing (7 types), planning (5 types), and acting (4 types). Drawing from cognitive neuroscience, psychology, communication studies, and human factors, each type addresses a distinct cognitive divergence that arises when users apply mechanisms evolved for understanding humans to robotic systems. The taxonomy’s exhaustiveness is established through a dimensional decomposition: three representational dimensions grounded in the neurocognitive architecture of human perception (What, Where, How) are systematically crossed with the three SPA processing stages, and every cell in the resulting matrix is accounted for by a dedicated type or an explicit justification. Each type is equipped with a formal definition and diagnostic examples. We demonstrate the taxonomy’s applicability across two contrasting datasets, TEACh (task-oriented simulation) and SHREC (social therapeutic dialogue), revealing distinct mismatch profiles that reflect the structural differences between the two settings. This taxonomy provides precise terminology enabling researchers to identify specific cognitive mismatches, and a foundation for developing targeted interventions, rather than treating all problems as generic “communication failures.”

candidates.title: Embodied Interaction Policy: A Unified Model for Full-Duplex Human-Robot Interaction
candidates.abstract: Real-time human-robot social interaction requires continuous coordination between speech and physical behavior. Existing systems often separate interaction agents from motion generation, complicating coordination as conversational states change. We propose \textbf{Embodied Interaction Policy (EIP)}, a unified streaming framework that couples an Audio-Interaction expert with a motion expert through layer-wise joint attention. This allows motion generation to directly access the evolving interaction context. A chunk-wise causal mask prevents access to future context, while a vocal token encodes speaking state and the semantic emotion of the response. We construct \textbf{Embodied Interaction Dataset (EI-Data)} from co-speech and dyadic interaction data and train our model in two stages to learn state-adaptive and emotion-conditioned behavior. Combined with the frozen interaction expert, EIP supports continuous robot motion during proactive responses and interruption-aware turn-taking. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate improved motion quality over representative gesture-generation baselines. Compared with a representative cascaded system, EIP achieves higher interaction success and reduces warm-start latency by 64\%. Physical deployment and user studies further demonstrate improved motion naturalness and interaction comfort.

candidates.title: To Bot or not To Bot: Integrating a Social Robot into the Actor’s Rehearsal Process
candidates.abstract: Effective theatrical rehearsal is essential for actors’ character development, involving intricate cognitive, emotional, and physical processes. Despite well-established traditional techniques that combine individual practice and partner interactions, rehearsal often requires significant time and resources. Emerging digital and robotic technologies present novel opportunities to enhance rehearsal methods; however, their potential as interactive rehearsal aids remains largely unexplored. This research examines the role of a social robot in supporting actors during pre-rehearsal or solo preparation of two scenes from Tennessee Williams’ The Glass Menagerie (1944). Thirty actors with different levels of experience participated in three rehearsal settings: solo practice, rehearsal with a robot playing one character, and rehearsal with the robot alternating between two roles. We evaluated the robot's impact via qualitative responses and self-reports. Thematic analysis indicated that robot-assisted rehearsal improved participants’ experience compared to solo rehearsal, especially among less experienced actors. The robot's role-switching capability offered additional depth appreciated mainly by seasoned performers. These outcomes highlight the promise of social robots as rehearsal tools adapted to the experience of actors.

candidates.title: Intent Representation and Human Distraction Modulate the Effects of Legible Robot Motion in Hallway Navigation
candidates.abstract: Legibility in human-robot interaction (HRI) is often described as the property of robot motion that enables an observer to confidently and quickly infer the robot’s intent. Mature frameworks exist for generating legible motion in front of static observers, typically by making the robot’s destination apparent as early as possible. Social robot navigation in public spaces, however, presents a different challenge: pedestrians are themselves in motion, often with divided attention, and must coordinate with the robot in real time. In such encounters, where the robot is ultimately headed may matter less to a pedestrian than how it intends to pass them. This raises two questions: which aspect of intent should legible motion convey, and does legibility remain beneficial when pedestrians are not fully attentive to the robot? We address these questions in the ubiquitous and demanding scenario of hallway navigation, through two controlled user studies comparing multiple legibility formulations implemented within a shared model predictive control framework. Study 1 (N = 45) compares destination-based and passing-side intent representations, showing that the latter, particularly when adaptively updated, allows for smoother human motion and is perceived as more competent and less mentally and physically demanding than the former. Study 2 (N = 45) examines the effect of pedestrian attention, demonstrating that legible motion supports smooth human motion even under distraction, although this benefit is not consistently reflected in subjective ratings. Together, these findings suggest that effective legible motion in social robot navigation benefits from interaction-level intent representations that support coordination, with some effects persisting even when human attention is divided. Code is available at https://github.com/fluentrobotics/Legible_MPPI and footage from our experiments at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P5O5BwfcUCo.

candidates.title: Kezek: Splitting Mono Two-Person Conversations into Per-Speaker Tracks for Full-Duplex Dialogue Data
candidates.abstract: Full-duplex spoken dialogue models learn turn-taking, overlaps and backchannels from conversations recorded with one channel per speaker, but most available conversational audio is a single mono mix. We present Kezek, a model that turns a mono recording of exactly two people into one track per person with the original length and timing; overlaps and short replies ("yeah", "mm-hm") stay on the track of the person who said them. Kezek decides who speaks when and who is who once for the whole recording (stage 1: a two-voice activity model guided by a speaker fingerprint trained to be insensitive to phase), and a conditioned time-domain separator only carries out that decision (stage 2), with outputs that always sum to the input. Standard separation metrics miss the failures that matter for dialogue data, so we report short-reply retention, leakage onto the other person's solo, channel swaps and coverage. Against the open pipeline pyannote -> DialogueSidon on the same recordings, Kezek keeps more short replies (0.83 vs. 0.69 on Open Yap test; 0.80 vs. 0.71 over the other's speech on unseen telephone speech from CallHome English), mostly because it returns the whole recording while the external pipeline drops part of it (on the audio both return, reply retention is about the same: 0.859 vs. 0.865 on Open Yap); it also leaks less, swaps channels less often, and runs 4-5 times faster (about 230 hours of audio per GPU-hour). We also report negative results and an ideal-mask ceiling that locate the remaining gap: quiet replies under a louder voice. Code and weights are released under permissive licences.

candidates.title: TinyML and Edge AI for On-Device Intelligence: A Review of Keyword Spotting and Voice-Controlled Assistive Robots
candidates.abstract: Voice is a natural control channel for assistive mobile robots. Yet most currently deployed voice interfaces stream audio to cloud-based recognizers, which adds latency, reliance on connectivity, and exposure of privacy. Tiny machine learning (TinyML) offers an alternative in which a quantized neural network performs keyword spotting (KWS) directly on a low-cost microcontroller. This review examines how far recent work from 2024 to 2026 supports the development of a voice-controlled assistive robot based on on-device KWS. We synthesize 40 recent studies covering compact KWS architectures, neural architecture search, quantization and pruning, noise and front-end variability, on-device personalization, speech-driven robotic systems, and safety-aware human-robot interaction. The literature indicates that efficient KWS models now fit within the memory and energy budgets of low-cost microcontrollers, and that personalization and open-set recognition are maturing. Evaluation practice, however, remains uneven: false activations per hour, end-to-end command-to-action latency, and energy per decision are seldom foregrounded, and few systems couple recognition confidence with motion safety logic. Building on these observations, we present a reference architecture for an ESP32-based assistive robot with six functional blocks, a confidence-aware command arbitration layer in which an emergency stop and obstacle checks take precedence over recognized speech, and a six-experiment evaluation protocol. Five distinct research gaps are identified, including speaker-independent validation, the effect of quantization on rare-command recall, and fail-safe behavior under sensor or model faults. The review rests on reported objectives and findings rather than reproduced experiments. It offers a structured basis for designing, benchmarking, and safely deploying offline voice-controlled assistive robots on resource-constrained hardware.

candidates.title: Enabling Proactive Spoken Turns via a Generalized Style-Aware Full-Duplex Framework
candidates.abstract: Compared with half-duplex dialogue systems where the system waits for user turn completion before it responds, natural full-duplex dialogue systems require agents to act proactively in real time, including timely interruptions and backchannels. This creates a key challenge: improving turn timing without sacrificing response quality. To address limitations in realistic proactive turn-taking, we build a generalized style-aware full-duplex framework with three key components. Firstly, we propose LPS-TC, a Lightweight Proactive Speech Turn Controller for plug-and-play integration. It features a fine-grained action space covering both reactive and proactive turn behaviors, enabling half-duplex models with full-duplex capabilities and enhancing existing full-duplex models with superior timing control. Secondly, we construct WildTurn, a large-scale, real-world English dataset containing approximately 2,981 hours of filtered multi-turn stereo conversations from face-to-face and telephone conversations, annotated with five turn-taking and five backchanneling styles. Trained on WildTurn, LPS-TC exhibits rich spoken dynamics that are not captured by existing static full-duplex benchmarks. Thirdly, we introduce a two-tier evaluation scheme that assesses both chunk-level timing precision and turn-level interaction quality under realistic streaming constraints. Our experiments, integrating LPS-TC with half-duplex models like Qwen2.5-Omni and full-duplex models like Freeze-Omni, showcase its superior performance in timing appropriateness and response quality. Our framework also demonstrates fine-grained style controllability and strong generalizability, enabling more natural and human-like spoken interactions.

candidates.title: Ethics and trust in social robot adoption for tourism: insights from Albania
candidates.abstract: Purpose Social robots are beginning to interact with guests in hotels, restaurants and tourist attractions, yet little is known about how travellers in emerging markets perceive their ethical implications or decide whether to trust them. This study aims to explore how participants in Albania evaluate the ethics of social robots and how these evaluations shape trust and adoption intention in tourism. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the technology acceptance model, the service robot acceptance model and the ethical awareness-trust framework, this study analysed responses from 205 surveyed young Albanians with recent travel experience and basic awareness of social/service robots, the majority of whom had STEM backgrounds. Respondents in this study rated perceived ethical risks, trust in social robots, perceived human-robot collaboration benefits, support for human oversight, perceived usefulness, human-likeness/emotional comfort, prior experience and familiarity and adoption intention. The study employed descriptive statistics, Spearman’s rank correlations, Hayes’ PROCESS macro for mediation and moderation, and Bayes fact or analysis. Findings Participants in this study reported the strongest concerns about inaccurate information and technical failures, alongside clear support for human involvement in decisions affecting guests. Ethical risk perception was strongly associated with support for human oversight (ρ = 0.747, p < 0.001). Trust was positively associated with perceived usefulness, human-likeness/emotional comfort, collaboration benefits, prior experience and familiarity. Mediation and moderation analyses showed that trust linked usefulness and human-likeness/emotional comfort to adoption intention, while perceived ethical risk reduced the extent to which trust translated into adoption intention. Overall, the findings point to a supervised, assistive model of social-robot use rather than autonomous replacement of human staff. Research limitations/implications This study provides focused evidence from Albania’s early-exposure tourism context, where social robots are still novel and expectations of trust, ethics and human oversight are emerging. Its cross-sectional design and respondent profile define the empirical setting of the analysis, while future research should test the trust-ethics model across more diverse traveller groups, longitudinal designs and destinations with different levels of social-robot exposure. Practical implications Hospitality providers should approach social-robot deployment as a supervised service model in which automation supports, rather than replaces, human responsibility. Practical use should prioritise reliable information, technical safety, transparent data practices and personalised assistance with clear routes for escalation to staff. Gradual implementation, supported by trust and safety monitoring, can help providers assess where robots add service value and where human involvement remains necessary. Originality/value This study advances service-robot acceptance research by investigating how perceived ethical risk influences the relationship between trust and adoption intention. This addresses a conceptual limitation in prior research, where technology-acceptance perspectives and AI/robot ethics perspectives have often been examined separately. By showing that trust may not fully translate into adoption intention when concerns about safety, privacy and human oversight are salient, this study clarifies how ethical risk shapes trust-based service-robot adoption in early-exposure tourism contexts.

candidates.title: The Effect of Robot’s Verbal Communication in Mixed-Hearing Ability Teams
candidates.abstract: Although robots show great potential as teammates, most researchers have focused on settings with a narrow view of possible human abilities, focusing on users without disabilities. Considering that verbal communication is one of the most widely used modalities in Human–Robot Interaction, its implications for teams composed of hearing and hard-of-hearing users remain underexplored. We set out to investigate this research gap by conducting an empirical study (N=16) in which a Tagi robot plays a collaborative game with two human participants, one is deaf or hard-of-hearing, and the other is hearing. We manipulated the communication modalities employed by the robot, verbal or non-verbal, in a within-subjects design. Our results showed that the verbal robot (compared to the non-verbal) sparked more non-verbal behaviours among participants, and that despite hearing participants perceived the robot as more animate and fair, deaf and hard of hearing participants felt more excluded. Finally, broader implications for social robots in mixed-hearing ability groups are discussed.

candidates.title: Design and Evaluation of an Emotionally Expressive Robotic Head, Woody for Socially Assistive Human–Robot Interaction.
candidates.abstract: Socially assistive robots offer a promising approach for communication training; however, many existing systems remain limited in expressive capability, interaction naturalness, and adaptive conversational intelligence. This paper presents Woody, an AI-enabled interactive robotic head intended for future evaluation in social interaction training through adaptive, multimodal human–robot engagement. The proposed platform integrates visual perception, facial expression recognition, speech processing, and a GPT-based dialogue agent to enable intelligent, real-time interactions. The engineering contribution is the coupling of conversational memory and multimodal cues with a custom 12-DOF expressive head. Its architecture emphasizes adaptive communication strategies, user-centered engagement, and behavioral feedback to encourage meaningful participation. Mechanically, Woody incorporates 12 degrees of freedom distributed across the eyes, eyelids, eyebrows, jaw, and neck, enabling expressive facial and head movements. The system provides eye-gaze shifts of ±35° in both axes, coordinated eyelid and eyebrow motions, jaw opening to 30°, and neck articulation with 90° yaw, +40°/−25° pitch, and ±40° roll. These capabilities allow the robot to convey natural facial expressions and nonverbal behaviors that enhance emotional communication. A preliminary adult evaluation assessed the feasibility of the proposed platform. Participants recognized Woody’s emotional expressions with 73% accuracy. During live interactions, the system achieved conversational response latencies of approximately 7–8 seconds, including perception, speech processing, and AI-based dialogue generation. A user study involving 32 adult participants reported high satisfaction in engagement (83%), patience (88%), and contextual relevance (93%). These findings indicate that Woody is a promising socially assistive robotic platform for future studies involving autism spectrum disorder (ASD) children's.

candidates.title: A Tinyml-Enabled Edge-Cloud Architecture for Multimodal Conversational AI
candidates.abstract: The convergence of Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) and cloud-hosted Large Language Models (LLMs) provides a transformative paradigm for intelligent edge computing, enabling microcontroller-class devices to deliver human-like conversational experiences without the prohibitive computational overhead of local foundation model execution. This paper presents the architecture, engineering deployment, and empirical evaluation of an advanced edge-assisted multimodal conversational agent built upon the UNIHIKER K10 single-board platform (powered by an Espressif ESP32-S3 dual-core SoC) and running the open-source xiaozhi-esp32 firmware framework integrated with the DeepSeek language reasoning model. Unlike conventional single-language microcontroller interfaces, the proposed system natively supports bilingual voice interaction in both English and Hindi with seamless code-switching, Devanagari acoustic handling, and contextual response generation.

candidates.title: AVCC: Audio-Visual Conversation Corpus for Turn-Taking Prediction with a Human Benchmark
candidates.abstract: } Predicting who will speak next, and when, is a prerequisite for conversational agents and social robots that take turns without waiting for silence. Multiparty next-speaker prediction (NSP) has been studied on corpora with per-speaker sensors, each with its own event definitions. No public benchmark covers the single camera and microphone a robot has, and no model has been compared against how well people perform the same prediction. We turn AVCC, a 31-hour audio-visual corpus of two- and three-speaker online conversation recorded with a single static camera and microphone, into a public NSP benchmark. We add a speaker-disjoint seven-video test partition with 865 hold and 865 shift events at mutual-silence gaps, word-level forced-aligned transcripts for the whole corpus, and a human reference benchmark collected at the same events. We score an audio-only Role-Relative VAP model (RoleVAP) and the multimodal MuVAP model. Labels, transcripts, per-response human data, and the scripts that reproduce every number are released.

candidates.title: Rapid Conversational Authoring of Interactive Human-Robot Activities
candidates.abstract: Social robots are being envisioned for a growing range of applications. Yet their behavior is still predominantly authored by robot experts and developers through hand-crafted interaction content or, more recently, large language model (LLM) prompts. This places control over robot behavior with those who implement the interaction rather than the domain experts and end users who better understand how the robot should serve users’ evolving needs over time. Existing end-user authoring tools, such as visual programming environments, lower this barrier but still require specialized authoring skills, including constructing interaction logic through blocks and flows. We present the Robot Interaction Development Environment (RIDE), an open-source, end-to-end, mobile-compatible system that automates much of the human-robot interaction authoring process. From a natural-language description of an activity, RIDE decomposes the interaction into a sequence of states, generates the interaction flow and state-level prompts that drive the robot, and deploys the resulting program. We evaluated RIDE through three case studies in which a speech language therapist designed social-skills practice for a patient, a high school French teacher designed conversation practice for a student, and a nurse designed a stress-relief activity for herself. All three participants created a deployable activity within seven conversational turns without writing prompts or program logic. While participants readily delegated interaction structure to the system, they retained control over domain-specific details such as target phrases and content to avoid. We discuss how low-effort, conversational authoring can enable domain experts and end users to rapidly adapt general-purpose social robots to their goals and evolving needs.

candidates.title: Real-Time Short-Response Selection for Spoken Dialogue Systems
candidates.abstract: To realize spoken dialogue systems that can interact naturally with users, it is important for the system to respond to user utterances at appropriate timings. To achieve such natural turn-taking, the system needs not only to predict appropriate response timings but also to mask delays caused by language generation and speech synthesis so that they are not perceived by the user. We propose a real-time short-response selection task that can be integrated with existing turn-taking models to mask generation delay. To address this task, the proposed model learns the mapping between dialogue context and short responses using contrastive learning. When a turn-taking event is detected, the system selects a response from a set of pre-generated candidates. The selected response is played while the main response is being generated. Experimental results show that the proposed method learns to select short responses based on dialogue context, outperforming random and LLM-based baselines. Moreover, integrating response selection maintained turn-taking prediction performance and added minimal processing overhead.

candidates.title: Cognitive and Affective Trust in Human–Robot Interaction: Effects on Task Delegation
candidates.abstract: Trust in Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) is a multidimensional construct involving both attitudes (cognitive and affective trust) and behavior (task delegation).In this paper, we experimentally separate the effects of robot competence, autonomy, and personality trait of agreeableness on cognitive trust, affective trust, and task delegation in a task-oriented HRI scenario.We report results from a 2×2×2 between-subjects study (N = 373) showing that competence is the primary driver of both trust attitudes and behavior, whereas personality affects affective trust without influencing delegation.Importantly, autonomy does not exert direct effects but acts as a contextual moderator, improving the impact of competence on cognitive trust and of personality on affective trust.We find that only cognitive trust predicts and mediates task delegation, while affective trust, despite being significantly modulated, does not translate into behavioral trust.These findings provide empirical evidence for a functional dissociation between affective and cognitive trust in HRI and highlight that behavioral trust is predominantly grounded in capability-based evaluations rather than affective factors.These findings clarify the distinct roles of functional and social robot attributes and provide insights for designing trustworthy and effective collaborative robots.

candidates.title: Design and Development of an AI-Based Voice-Controlled Robot for Intelligent Human-Robot Interaction
candidates.abstract: Most low-cost voice-controlled robots accept only a handful of fixed words such as “forward” and “stop”, and depend on a smartphone app for speech recognition. This paper presents the design and development of an AI-based voice-controlled mobile robot that holds natural spoken conversations and turns free-form requests into safe movements. The robot is built around an ESP32 microcontroller with an INMP441 I²S MEMS microphone, a MAX98357A I²S class-D amplifier and speaker, an L298N dual H-bridge driving two DC gear motors with wheels, a servo for head and gesture movements, and a 2S pack of 18650 lithium-ion cells with a main switch. A hybrid architecture is used: a compact keyword-spotting model on the ESP32 detects the wake word and a local “stop” command without any network, while the spoken request is streamed to an AI server where speech-to-text, a large language model and text-to-speech produce a structured JSON action and a spoken reply. A command validator on the ESP32 checks every action against a whitelist, speed limits and a time-out before the motors move, so the language model can never drive the robot outside its safe envelope. A review of 19 related studies shows that earlier robots offered either fixed-vocabulary control on cheap hardware or natural-language interaction on expensive platforms, but rarely both. Design calculations show that a 4-second request needs 128 kB of audio, well within the ESP32's memory, and that the battery pack supports an estimated 13.4 h of mixed use. An experimental protocol with metrics for recognition accuracy, latency, safety response and user experience is provided for prototype validation.

candidates.title: Sensing What Children Feel: A Multimodal Approach to Emotion Recognition in Child-Robot Interaction
candidates.abstract: Socially assistive robots can support children’s learning, therapy, and emotional development, but only if they reliably perceive children’s affective states. Existing emotion-recognition systems are largely designed for adults and rely mainly on facial expressions, which are variable in children. We investigate affective sensing in child–robot interaction (CRI) as a design problem by developing a game-based interaction to elicit joy, disappointment, and neutral states. Synchronous facial and physiological signals were collected from 27 children interacting with a simulated NAO robot. Under leave-one-subject-out evaluation, a late-fusion model combining both modalities outperformed either modality alone (66.67% vs. 58.33% facial, 53.70% physiological), with gains driven by the two modalities’ complementary error patterns on disappointment, the state where adaptive robot support matters most. Disappointment, a key state for adaptive support, was detected least accurately due to limited visible expression. Initially, fusion with a weak physiological branch fell 6.48 points below the facial baseline, recovering only after that branch was strengthened. Results highlight that effective CRI emotion recognition depends on interaction design and modality quality as much as model choice.

candidates.title: Duopra: From Full-Duplex Conversation to Full-Duplex Agency
candidates.abstract: Full-duplex interaction models exhibit strong conversational agency, enabling natural, low-latency turn-taking, backchannels, and interruptions. However, completing tasks further requires task agency: timely tool invocation and argument revision following user corrections. Frontend-backend agents separate initiation from execution: the frontend decides whether and what to request, while the backend determines how. Execution can be offloaded, but unsent requests cannot be executed, and incomplete ones can misdirect the backend. On Full-Duplex-Bench v3 (FDB v3), most failures of Realtime-Venus-Audio + Harness in our streaming pipeline occur before a domain tool executes. We introduce Duopra, a full-duplex interaction model that learns task execution alongside conversational control. Duopra treats the backend as a tool, accepting a self-contained natural-language request. Direct calls and backend delegation share an action interface and requirements for faithful initiation and correct execution. Its three-stage training combines protocol SFT, full-duplex RL rewarding timely and complete execution, and projector-only repair of talker conditioning after thinker updates. With the same backend, Pass@1 rises from 4.7% to 44.7%; Duopra achieves 47.7% calling tools directly (26.0% after SFT) and 49.3% with a DeepSeek backend. It improves three FDB v1.0 takeover rates over the base model. These results show that task agency can coexist with key conversational agency.

candidates.title: Latency, Speech Recognition and Turn-Taking in Voice Agents for Spanish Phone Negotiation: An Externally Measured Comparison of Pipecat, LiveKit and GPT-Live
candidates.abstract: A voice agent that negotiates by phone must answer quickly, understand spoken amounts and cope with a caller who talks over it. We compared three architectures for such an agent, negotiating freight rates in Spanish: two cascades (speech recognition, language model and speech synthesis) orchestrated by Pipecat and by LiveKit Agents, and GPT-Live, an OpenAI speech model that listens and speaks without separate stages. A program played the carrier with the same 47 recordings of one speaker for all agents, without the telephone network, in 77 calls per architecture over five negotiation scenarios, and measured latency on the listener's side with a validated instrument. Median latency to the content response was 2,616.0 ms (Pipecat), 3,090.0 ms (LiveKit) and 2,444.8 ms (GPT-Live); the confidence interval of GPT-Live's 171.2 ms advantage over Pipecat includes zero. According to its own timestamps, GPT-Live began to answer 800 ms after the end of the line, close to the 0.8 s published by OpenAI; most of the remaining wait, about 1,367 ms and nearly constant, is the audio's round trip through OpenAI's service. A tool call added 0.9-1.1 s in every architecture, more than any difference between them, and the frameworks' self-reported latency fell short of the listener's wait by 9% (Pipecat) and 22% (LiveKit). Word error rates were low (6.03, 4.93 and 1.47%), but the error on amounts was 13.01% and 12.61% in the cascades, against 2.86% in GPT-Live. With default settings, Pipecat and LiveKit stopped at almost every backchannel and often took it as the carrier's answer: an "ok" spoken over the agent ended in a registered agreement in 3 of 15 Pipecat calls, 2 of 15 LiveKit calls and no GPT-Live call (descriptive counts, not tested). Latency should therefore be measured on the listener's side, and a cascade needs safeguards for spoken amounts and backchannels.

candidates.title: Adapting Affect Perception Across Users: Continual Facial Expression Recognition in Human--Robot Interaction
candidates.abstract: Facial expression recognition (FER) is important for socially adaptive human–robot interaction, yet models trained on static datasets may struggle when encountering users with different facial characteristics and expression styles. We investigate continual user adaptation for robot-perceived FER using the Robot-Perceived Facial Expression Recognition (RPFER) dataset, collected from the viewpoint of a social robot during turn-based interactions with 22 participants. Each participant is treated as a sequential domain while the six emotion classes remain fixed, which requires the model to adapt to newly encountered users while retaining performance on previously observed users. We propose and evaluate representative continual learning approaches, including regularization and replay-based methods, under this participant-incremental setting. Results show that replay-based approaches consistently outperform regularization-only methods, with performance improving as replay memory increases. In addition to Average Accuracy Performance, Backward Transfer, and Forgetting, we evaluate the Coefficient of Variation of Individual Accuracies (CVIA) to characterize performance consistency across users. These results highlight the importance of continual adaptation and user-level reliability for affect perception in long-term human-robot interaction.

candidates.title: Leveraging Dual-Process Theory for Multimodal Multiparty Turn-Taking Prediction
candidates.abstract: In multiparty conversations, a pause does not always mean a speaker has finished, and another voice does not necessarily indicate a change in who holds the conversational floor. Reliable turn-taking therefore requires recognising not only whether a speaker is ready to yield the floor, but also when a possible transition deserves attention. We propose a dual-process-inspired framework that separates continuous candidate discovery from selective verification. A fast, recall-oriented stage identifies plausible transition points. In contrast, a deliberative stage combines acoustic, linguistic, speaker-related, and predicted future-activity evidence, together with multimodal cues where available, to reject false candidates and refine transition timing. We evaluate the framework through three distinct tasks: SHIFT/HOLD classification at supplied decision points, verification of automatically generated candidates, and continuous discovery and localisation of floor transfers. On VoxConverse, we derive action-aware turn-taking events from speaker-diarization annotations to examine unconstrained conversations with varying numbers of speakers. Multi-TPC provides complementary evaluation of controlled triadic interactions using speech, gaze, motion, and prosodic information. The findings reveal that identifying plausible transitions is considerably easier than reliably confirming and localising genuine floor transfers, while the contribution of individual evidence sources varies across conversational settings. These results highlight the importance of treating multiparty turn-taking as a continuous discovery-and-verification problem rather than classification at predefined boundaries.

candidates.title: Participatory design in human-robot interaction research: a systematic review
candidates.abstract: Participatory Design (PD) approaches for robot design offer promising avenues for enhancing technological innovation and aligning Human–Robot Interaction (HRI) systems with user needs. Despite their potential, there is a lack of a comprehensive overview of how these approaches have been utilized within the field of HRI. This article presents a systematic review of the literature on how PD is applied in the design of HRI systems, highlighting its advantages and challenges. Data were collected by reviewing 102 selected articles published from 2008 to 2024 in leading scientific databases for robotics. We summarize and classify the selected PD studies based on stakeholder participation, methods, and outcomes, among other aspects. We also report on the contributions of PD methodologies to key HRI issues, including ethical challenges, robot autonomy, and human-robot conflicts. Findings show a growing number of HRI researchers using PD approaches, particularly in the context of social robots for healthcare and assistive services. However, we also found that a perspective where robots are considered the solution to every problem, without fully understanding the realities of the target community, is still prevalent and that some aspects of PD, such as equalizing power relations, situated-based action, and long-term stakeholder engagement, are often overlooked.

candidates.title: Sound Classification for Non-Verbal Human-Robot Interaction
candidates.abstract: Schall ist eine schnelle, intuitive Modalität der Mensch–Roboter-Interaktion (HRI). Die robuste Echtzeitklassifikation strukturierter nonverbaler Geräusche, etwa Buzzertöne, in authentischen Klassenräumen bleibt jedoch schwierig. Kurze, transiente und nahezu simultane Ereignisse in einkanaligen Aufnahmen werden von etablierten Machine-Learning- und Deep-Learning-Verfahren nur eingeschränkt zuverlässig verarbeitet, und es fehlt ein Rahmen, der die Qualität robotischer Wahrnehmung mit dem motivationalen Erleben Lernender verbindet. Die Dissertation untersucht (RQ1), wie eine genaue und stabile Echtzeitklassifikation unter Klassenraumbedingungen erreicht werden kann, (RQ2), wie ein modulares Framework mehrere Klassifikationsansätze mit multimodalem Roboterfeedback integriert, und (RQ3), wie Variationen der Wahrnehmungszuverlässigkeit mit dem motivationalen Erleben zusammenhängen. Ein Vergleich von CRNN mit Attention, Random Forest und signalverarbeitungsbasierten Verfahren zeigt, dass Deep-Learning-Modelle im Labor sehr hohe Genauigkeiten erreichen, unter Echtzeitbedingungen und Domänenverschiebung jedoch nachlassen, während ein vorlagenbasierter Cross-Korrelations-Ansatz stabil bleibt. Das Sound Interaction Framework (SIF) integriert diese Verfahren und bildet Erkennungsergebnisse auf Roboterverhalten ab. Es wurde in fünf Design-Based-Research-Studien mit Studierenden iterativ weiterentwickelt und evaluiert. Stabilere Wahrnehmung war konsistent mit flüssigerer Interaktion, höher wahrgenommener Fairness und positiverer Motivation assoziiert. Darauf aufbauend wird die Algorithmic Precision–Motivation Relationship (APMR) als designorientiertes Modell ohne Anspruch auf deterministische Kausalität vorgeschlagen. Beiträge: (1) ein effizienter Ansatz für soundbasiertes Turn-Taking, (2) ein modulares Framework für soundgetriebene Bildungsroboter und (3) eine empirisch fundierte konzeptionelle Synthese von Wahrnehmungszuverlässigkeit und Interaktionserleben.

candidates.title: The Color of Emotions: a Culturally-Aware Visual Emotional Regulation Architecture for Social Robotics
candidates.abstract: Socially assistive robots increasingly rely on Facial Expression Recognition (FER) to perceive the affective state of their users, yet most systems stop at recognition and react in a culturally "one-size-fits-all" manner.Because they are trained predominantly on WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) data, they treat the symbolic meaning of colors and emotions as universal, even though this meaning is a culturally learned construct.We present the Visual Emotional Regulation System (VERS), a modular, device-agnostic architecture that dissociates perception (treated, as a deliberate operational assumption, as largely universal) from signification (which is culture-specific).A perceptual module recognizes the user's emotion from facial expressions; a cultural-clustering module maps a declared nationality to a macro-cluster; and a chromatic-actuation module composes a regulating color by passing a culture-free regulatory intent through the user's culture-specific symbolic code, verbalized through an inner-speech layer that grants cognitive transparency, rendering each cultural assumption inspectable and revisable.A systematic, data-centric comparison of five vision backbones across three datasets shows that data quality dominates architectural depth, with a Swin Transformer trained on a large, class-balanced corpus clearly outperforming deeper but data-starved alternatives.Crucially, the regulating color is not read from a lookup table but composed at each cycle from a culture-free intent and a culture-specific symbolic code, so that identical detected emotions yield culturally-differentiated colors, each delivered together with its verbalized rationale.A real-time prototype illustrates this behavior in a preliminary, two-participant proof-of-concept A/B demonstration, in which the same detected emotion is regulated with different, culturally-licensed hues; a protocol for large-scale cross-cultural validation is defined and left to future work.We chart the limits of macro-cluster reasoning and outline a path toward micro-adaptive, biometrically closed-loop regulation.VERS thus reframes affective robotics as a problem of meaning, not merely of recognition.

candidates.title: Participatory design in human-robot interaction research: a systematic review
candidates.abstract: Participatory Design (PD) approaches for robot design offer promising avenues for enhancing technological innovation and aligning Human–Robot Interaction (HRI) systems with user needs. Despite their potential, there is a lack of a comprehensive overview of how these approaches have been utilized within the field of HRI. This article presents a systematic review of the literature on how PD is applied in the design of HRI systems, highlighting its advantages and challenges. Data were collected by reviewing 102 selected articles published from 2008 to 2024 in leading scientific databases for robotics. We summarize and classify the selected PD studies based on stakeholder participation, methods, and outcomes, among other aspects. We also report on the contributions of PD methodologies to key HRI issues, including ethical challenges, robot autonomy, and human-robot conflicts. Findings show a growing number of HRI researchers using PD approaches, particularly in the context of social robots for healthcare and assistive services. However, we also found that a perspective where robots are considered the solution to every problem, without fully understanding the realities of the target community, is still prevalent and that some aspects of PD, such as equalizing power relations, situated-based action, and long-term stakeholder engagement, are often overlooked.

candidates.title: HEIR: Harness Egocentric Intent for Human-Robot Interactions
candidates.abstract: For robots to assist, serve, and collaborate with humans, they must not only interpret human requests conveyed through language and multimodal intentional cues, but also execute long-horizon tasks that interleave navigation and manipulation. In this paper, we introduce HEIR, a resource for studying how to Harness Egocentric Intent for Human-Robot Interaction. HEIR pairs human speech, measured gaze, and egocentric video with robot observations and teleoperated navigation-manipulation trajectories, while each session preserves successive episodes, with each request fulfilled through multiple execution subtasks. The captured data, together with human-authored annotations, support the study of intent grounding, execution planning, and task completion within a unified interaction setting. To demonstrate the value of HEIR, we conduct extensive offline experiments to evaluate how models benefit from additional human-centric context across these tasks, together with real-robot experiments that assess execution task completion. HEIR thus provides a valuable resource for studying user-centric robot interaction in naturalistic household environments. Our demo and dataset are available online.

candidates.title: When a feature becomes a bug: evolutionary mismatch in human–robot interaction
candidates.abstract: As robots become increasingly integrated into everyday life, evolved psychological mechanisms originally adapted for human social interaction may shape responses to artificial agents in ways that are no longer functionally appropriate. Drawing on an evolutionary psychology framework, the present study examined how anthropomorphism, empathy, and systemizing influence decisions involving a humanoid home robot. Participants (N = 519) completed an online experiment in which they viewed one of six robot stimuli varying in appearance (human-like, ambiguous, or robotic) and gender (female or male). They then read a scenario in which the manufacturer instructed them to reset the malfunctioning robot, thereby erasing its memories, while the robot pleaded not to be deactivated. Participants rated their willingness to deactivate the robot and the anticipated discomfort associated with doing so, and subsequently completed measures of anthropomorphism, empathy, and systemizing. Two 2 × 3 general linear models showed that stronger anthropomorphic tendencies predicted lower willingness to deactivate the robot, whereas higher systemizing predicted greater willingness. Empathy did not predict the decision itself but was associated with greater anticipated discomfort, together with anthropomorphism, while systemizing predicted lower discomfort. Contrary to our expectations, the decision to deactivate the robot did not vary as a function of its appearance. However, robot appearance influenced anticipated discomfort through interaction effects. These findings suggest that distinct evolved psychological mechanisms differentially shape behavioral and emotional responses to humanoid robots, consistent with the notion that evolutionary mismatch is at play human-robot interactions.

candidates.title: Development of a Triboelectric Nanogenerator-Based Sensory System for Human–Robot Interaction Detection
candidates.abstract: The translation of triboelectric tactile sensing from laboratory demonstrations to operational robotic platforms remains limited by high-impedance signal acquisition, mechanical integration, surface coverings, and robot-induced disturbances. Herein, we design a TENG-based sensing approach towards embodied robotic perception by demonstrating an end-to-end tactile interface that converts human touch into behavior-ready information within JARI, a modular social robot. The proposed system combines spatially distributed single-electrode and contact-separation triboelectric nanogenerators to encode the intensity, temporal dynamics, and spatial extent of physical interactions. Two-channel signals are acquired through a high-impedance interface, digitized by an ESP32 and transmitted (via Bluetooth or wired serial) directly to a desktop computer, where CNN-BiLSTM inference and ROS 2 communication are performed. A hybrid convolutional and bidirectional long short-term memory network classifies five tactile states: no contact, finger stroke, hand stroke, finger tap, and hand tap. The resulting states are published through ROS 2 and mapped to differentiated expressive responses, closing the perception-to-behavior loop. Unlike conventional bench-top evaluations, the system was assessed after the sensors were physically mounted on JARI, under stationary and moving conditions, to test the influence of fabrics on the sensor configurations. Battery-powered Bluetooth acquisition was associated with improved signal integrity compared with wired serial acquisition. The system achieved condition-specific accuracies of up to 94.8% when integrated into the stationary robot and up to 90.6% during robot motion. The alternative textile configuration yielded accuracies of 92.0% at rest and 85.0% during motion. Because each deployment condition was evaluated using independently acquired datasets, condition-specific preprocessing parameters, and separately trained models, these results should be interpreted as evidence of feasibility under the evaluated operating conditions rather than as a direct benchmark of performance across conditions. Neural inference on the desktop computer required 0.73–1.74 ms per prepared sequence. These results demonstrate that robust TENG-based tactile perception depends on the joint design of the sensor, mechanical interface, acquisition electronics, and intelligent processing architecture. The proposed framework establishes a practical route from self-generated triboelectric signals to real-time, context-aware physical interaction in social and assistive robotics.

candidates.title: Rhythmic-Semantic Co-Speech Gestures for Emotional Dialogue in Robots
candidates.abstract: Most data-driven robot systems generate either rhythmic beat-like motion or semantically meaningful iconic gestures, but not both. We present an emotion-aware rhythmic–semantic co-speech gesture system that generates iconic and beat behaviors in real time from text and the robot’s internal emotional state. We propose lightweight models that predict iconic timing and intensity, then fill the remaining spans with emotion-conditioned beats. We train on BEAT2 and deploy on the social robot Haru. In an online user study (N = 60), our method shows stronger speech–gesture alignment and is preferred over baselines.

candidates.title: When robots should look away: how gaze direction and anthropomorphism shape psychological responses to human-robot interaction in embarrassing service encounters
candidates.abstract: Compared with human providers, service robots can alleviate consumer discomfort in embarrassing service encounters, while their social cues shape responses. As robots’ facial design becomes increasingly sophisticated, gaze direction is a social cue in human-robot interaction (HRI), yet its role in embarrassing encounters across levels of anthropomorphism remains unclear. These effects matter for socially adaptive robot design. Grounded in the Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) paradigm, this research examined how robot gaze direction (direct vs. averted) and anthropomorphism (high vs. low) influence consumer continuance intention in embarrassing service encounters. Three between-subjects experiments were conducted ( N = 1,200). Study 1 examined this interaction across embarrassing and non-embarrassing contexts, while Studies 2 and 3 investigated the mediating roles of perceived warmth and competence; Study 3 additionally examined neuroticism as a potential moderator. Data were analyzed using factorial ANOVA and conditional process analysis. Across all three studies, the effect of gaze direction on continuance intention depended on robot anthropomorphism in embarrassing service encounters. Under high anthropomorphism, averted gaze led to higher continuance intention than direct gaze, whereas the opposite pattern emerged under low anthropomorphism. Study 1 further revealed a significant three-way interaction involving service context, with the gaze direction × anthropomorphism interaction reaching significance in embarrassing but not non-embarrassing service encounters. Studies 2 and 3 identified two distinct psychological pathways in embarrassing service encounters: averted gaze enhanced continuance intention by reducing perceived warmth under high anthropomorphism, whereas direct gaze did so by increasing perceived competence under low anthropomorphism. In Study 3, neuroticism did not significantly moderate the interaction between gaze direction and anthropomorphism in embarrassing service encounters. This research demonstrates that the interaction between robot gaze direction and anthropomorphism varies across embarrassing and non-embarrassing contexts, refining understanding of how robot social cues shape consumer responses. It extends the warmth and competence framework by revealing distinct perception pathways across anthropomorphism levels and showing that perceived warmth may inhibit continuance intention in embarrassing consumption contexts. These findings offer practical guidance for configuring robot gaze direction according to anthropomorphism in embarrassing service encounters.

candidates.title: Unconvincing Realism: The Experience of Alterity and the Art of Character Design in Conversational Agents and Social Robots

candidates.title: Rhythmic-Semantic Co-Speech Gestures for Emotional Dialogue in Robots
candidates.abstract: Co-speech gestures can increase engagement and improve speech understanding. Yet, most data-driven robot systems generate either rhythmic beat-like motion or semantically meaningful iconic gestures, but not both. We present an emotion-aware rhythmic-semantic co-speech gesture system that generates iconic and beat behaviors in real time from text and the robot's internal emotional state. We formalize the task of beat-iconic gesture generation using emotion and propose lightweight models that predict iconic timing and intensity, then fill the remaining spans with emotion-conditioned beats at an appropriate intensity level. We train on the BEAT2 dataset and deploy the system on the social robot Haru. In an online user study with 60 participants, our method shows stronger speech-gesture alignment and is preferred over baseline methods.

candidates.title: Evaluating Human-Robot Interaction With a Socially Assistive Robot in Pediatric Health Care: Mixed Methods Pilot Study
candidates.abstract: Background: Socially assistive robots are increasingly explored in health care, but evidence from routine pediatric outpatient settings remains limited. Objective: This study examined how contextual support and human facilitation shaped visitor interaction with the Temi V3 robot and which sociotechnical conditions were associated with practical acceptance according to staff. Methods: A mixed methods pilot combined structured behavioral observation across baseline, poster support, and staff facilitation conditions with 4 staff focus group interviews. The observation unit was a visitor passage through the lobby zone; the qualitative sample comprised 12 staff members with direct exposure to the robot. Quantitative indicators were analyzed descriptively, and staff interviews underwent deductive-inductive qualitative content analysis. Results: In total, 675 visitor passages (children: n=398, 59% and adults: n=277, 41%) were recorded (baseline: n=257; poster support: n=160; and staff facilitation: n=258). Looking at the robot increased from 8 (3.1%) passages at baseline to 30 (18.8%) with poster support and 80 (31%) with staff facilitation. Screen or app use increased from 2 (0.8%) passages at baseline to 4 (2.5%) with poster support and 14 (5.4%) with staff facilitation. Observer notes indicated stronger visible responsiveness among children, although age category was not linked to individual behavior codes. Staff emphasized role clarity, child and family value, human mediation, functional reliability, multilingual content, and organizational ownership. Conclusions: Observed visitor interaction was higher with poster support and staff facilitation than at baseline. These descriptive findings and staff perceptions informed a provisional 4-domain framework comprising role clarity, interaction affordance, social mediation, and organizational embedding. The framework identifies potential implementation priorities; visitors' own experiences and acceptance require direct assessment.

candidates.title: “Social” artificial intelligence? When interactions with AI conversational agents feel social and why it matters
candidates.abstract: Interactions with conversational AI agents powered by large language models (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude) vary considerably in the extent to which they are experienced as "social" in nature. The same system, for example, might be experienced as nonsocial when used to retrieve information, but as more social when used for emotional support. However, little is known about what shapes these perceptions of sociality or why they matter for human connection and well-being. Here, we discuss likely antecedents and consequences of perceived AI sociality. First, we propose that perceived sociality emerges jointly from characteristics of the AI (e.g., memory), the human perceiver (e.g., mind attribution), and the human-AI interaction itself (e.g., purpose of the interaction). Second, we hypothesize that greater perceived sociality amplifies both the potential benefits and risks of interacting with AI: as the interaction feels more social, users may experience greater perceived responsiveness and emotional support, but simultaneously feel greater attachment and vulnerability to influence or loss. Perceived sociality is also likely to shape how interacting with AI affects human-human relationships, including whether AI supplements or substitutes for human connection, affects users' interpersonal skills, and recalibrates expectations for human relationships. Ultimately, understanding when and why AI feels social is critical for evaluating its implications for human connection and well-being.

candidates.title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open and Efficient Small Language Model for Fast Conversational Agents
candidates.abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open and efficient small language model further post-trained from Gemma-4-E4B-it and optimized for speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for fast conversational agents. The model carries forward Gemma's strong conversational capabilities and further improves multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding for fast, local voice/device assistants, interactive personas, and embedded/Edge interfaces. The model combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power voice/device assistants, interactive characters and robotic/IoT interfaces running on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. Experiments on 21 benchmarks show that Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB achieves the highest average accuracy while generating the fewest output tokens in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes, compared with Gemma-4-E4B-it and Qwen3.5-4B. The model is released with a DFlash drafter. With DFlash, Bolt E4B achieves $2.74\times$ the per-user decode speed of inference without speculative decoding at concurrency~1, and $1.21\times$ the generation throughput of Gemma-4-E4B-it with MTP at batch size 1.

candidates.title: TinyML and Embedded Artificial Intelligence for Intelligent, Healthcare, Speech Processing, and Assistive Applications: A Comprehensive Review
candidates.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) are key technologies for creating intelligent systems in healthcare, speech processing, assistive technology, IoT, and other areas. Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) enables ML models to run on microcontrollers with extremely limited computing, memory and power resources. In this research, we will look at intelligent edge systems and various challenges associated with them, such as computing constraints, model complexity and real-time requirements, as well as tradeoffs with energy, data security, and privacy. We also look at the challenges with cloud-based AI systems for healthcare and assistive technology. We will perform a literature review on TinyML and other embedded AI systems for constrained and resource-poor environments. We will look at different techniques to reduce the size of AI systems and to train them to run on resource-constrained systems. We will also look at other intelligent systems in speech, language and communication technologies for people with speech and language disabilities. We will look at different intelligent systems for healthcare and rehabilitation. Finally, we look at various technologies for the IoT, including intelligent systems with embedded intelligence for real-time analysis and decision making. We look at various types of intelligent systems and AI technologies, as well as the issues associated with integrating and deploying them in the real world. We look at barriers including reliability, security, privacy, and the tradeoffs with real-world deployment. We also look at various research approaches and evaluation criteria. We will propose plans of actions and research guidelines for developing more secure, explainable, and energy-efficient AI systems.

candidates.title: Robot social anxiety as a distinct psychological construct: Relations to human social anxiety and development of the multidimensional social robot anxiety scale
candidates.abstract: Anxiety toward social robots is becoming increasingly relevant as they enter everyday environments; however, the psychological structure of this anxiety and its relation to interpersonal social anxiety remain unclear. This study developed and validated the Multidimensional Social Robot Anxiety Scale (MSRAS) and examined whether robot social anxiety (RSA) constituted a distinct psychological construct via two large-scale surveys (N 1 = 1,957; N 2 = 2,393). Based on Dennett’s framework, factor-analytic results identified four dimensions: Physical Danger, Social Cognitive Ability, Information Security, and Social Anxiety toward Robots. These were supported by a bifactor structure in which RSA retained substantial unique variance, indicating that it was conceptually and empirically distinct from other robot-related anxieties. Furthermore, structural equation modeling revealed that general human social anxiety significantly predicted RSA, suggesting that RSA and human social anxiety (HSA) share certain psychological characteristics. However, RSA diverged from HSA in its socio-emotional correlates: it had markedly weaker associations with self-perceived social skills and perceived social support. The association between RSA and need to belong was weaker than that with social phobia but comparable to that with social interaction anxiety, providing only partial support for the predicted attenuation of belongingness-related concerns. These findings suggest that RSA and HSA share certain characteristics while exhibiting systematic differences, potentially reflecting the perceived limitations of robots' social-evaluative and emotional capacities. Furthermore, the MSRAS is a psychometrically robust tool for examining individual differences in robot-related anxiety and advancing theoretical models of anxiety in human–robot interactions.

candidates.title: A Comprehensive Analysis of Artificial Intelligence Based Human Robot Interaction for Healthcare Monitoring
candidates.abstract: The artificial intelligence technology is advancing at a rapid pace, and it is transforming the manner in which robots perform. Due to artificial intelligence, machines are increasingly becoming capable of performing hard work that requires much thought and physical labour in locations where people live and work. The paper is on the subject of considering how artificial intelligences in the human and robot interaction particularly in the healthcare sector can be discussed. It borrows data on research, new innovations and current technology to understand how artificial intelligence robots are being utilized in hospitals to attend to patients and assist them in recovering and simplify the work of hospitals. The use of artificial intelligence is applied in practice, patient care, rehabilitation and hospital operations. The machine learning and computer vision and language processing and sensor-driven control are things which assist a robot to know what it is around to make good decisions and talk to people in a good way. The paper also discusses the evolution of healthcare robotics over the years where machines used to assist people or help them in surgery, to the present machines which can act independently and engage people. Additionally, ethical, safety and social issues concerning the application of intelligent robots in the medical context are considered as well as transparency, trust and human centric design perceived as essential elements. This paper properly describes the future of robotic systems in healthcare monitoring and human robot interaction using artificial intelligence by combining technological advances and trends in applications.

candidates.title: Social Robots
candidates.abstract: This chapter examines social robots as a physiological component of the robonomic system, focusing on their emergence as embodied interfaces through which artificial intelligence enters everyday human environments. It traces the conceptual evolution of the term social robots , from early speculative uses to a stabilised interaction-oriented meaning within contemporary robotics. Two research trajectories are reconstructed: one rooted in collective and self-organising robot–robot systems, and the other in humanoid and developmental robotics centred on human–robot interaction. Their convergence produced a paradigm in which social robots are defined not by morphology but by their capacity to engage humans through socially meaningful behaviour shaped by cultural norms. The chapter combines conceptual and scientometric analysis to document the consolidation of social robotics as a recognised research domain. Particular attention is devoted to behavioural alignment as a condition for socioeconomic integration. Unlike industrial robots operating in controlled settings, social robots act in open, normatively structured environments, where misalignment may affect public trust, regulation, and diffusion. The chapter concludes by examining care and service contexts as critical tests of alignment, highlighting how social robots challenge established boundaries between tools, social actors, and institutions.

candidates.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN CREATIVE INDUSTRIES: A CONCEPTUAL REVIEW OF CREATIVE ROBOTICS AND HUMAN-ROBOT INTERACTION
candidates.abstract: This conceptual paper critically examines how artificial intelligence (AI) connects creative industries, creative robotics, and human–robot interaction (HRI). Although AI-assisted cultural production is widely discussed, the relationship between software-based content generation and physically embodied robotic collaboration remains insufficiently differentiated. Drawing on a critical, purposively selected literature base spanning computational creativity, media production, socio-technical studies, and HRI, the paper develops an interpretive synthesis of four dimensions: creative augmentation; embodied co-creation; creative agency, labour, and authorship; and ethical governance and cultural sustainability. The literature suggests that AI can support ideation, generation, adaptive feedback, and interactive creation, although implications for originality, professional authority, and participation depend on context. Unlike software-only applications, creative robots introduce spatial coordination, material action, and reciprocal feedback into artistic activity. The paper advances a socio-technical framework distinguishing these modes of collaboration and linking them to institutional and cultural conditions. Practical implications concern human-centred workflow design, transparent attribution, interdisciplinary education, and inclusive governance. The framework is an analytical proposition rather than an empirically validated model; its application requires further workplace and HRI research.

candidates.title: TurnTurk-GPT: Text-Based Turn-Taking Prediction for Turkish
candidates.abstract: This paper presents TurnTurk-GPT, a text-based turn-taking predictor for Turkish obtained by fine-tuning a Turkish GPT-2 model with the TurnGPT objective on synthetic and real dialogue, and evaluates it on real Turkish conversation against rule baselines, a zero shot Turkish language model and a widely used multilingual end-of-turn detector. Evaluation uses word-level decision points on unpunctuated, lower-cased text approximating the output of streaming speech recognisers, recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint folds, nested threshold selection and paired cluster bootstrap tests. TurnTurk-GPT outperforms the multilingual detector under both recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint evaluation. Its gain over a zero-shot Turkish language model is largest for speakers seen in training, while on unseen speakers it matches this strong baseline. Removing the suffixes of the turn-final word reduces AP by up to 44%, against 2% for a sentence-internal word, locating the Turkish end-of-turn cue in verb-final morphology. Synthetic dialogue alone yields the weakest trained model, and when a speaker pauses the zero-shot and multilingual baselines remain close to chance. The model and the evaluation protocol are publicly released.

candidates.title: StretchBot: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Adaptive Guidance with Assistive Robots
candidates.abstract: Assistive robots have growing potential to support physical wellbeing in home and healthcare settings, for example, by guiding users through stretching or rehabilitation routines. However, existing systems remain largely scripted, which limits their ability to adapt to user state, environmental context, and interaction dynamics. In this work, we present StretchBot, a hybrid neuro-symbolic robotic coach for adaptive assistive guidance. The system combines multimodal perception with knowledge-graph-grounded large language model reasoning to support context-aware adjustments during short stretching sessions while maintaining a structured routine. To complement the system description, we report an exploratory pilot comparison between scripted and adaptive guidance with three participants. The pilot observations indicate that the adaptive condition was rated higher for perceived adaptability and contextual relevance, while scripted guidance remained competitive in smoothness and predictability. These observations suggest that structured actionable knowledge may help ground language-model-based adaptation in embodied assistive interaction, while highlighting the need for larger, longitudinal studies to evaluate robustness, generalizability, and long-term user experience.

candidates.title: Enabling gesture recognition on a resource-constrained device: a TinyML approach with envelope EMG data and real-time testing
candidates.abstract: Gesture recognition from electromyography (EMG) is used to control prostheses and rehabilitation devices, but real-time classifiers must balance accuracy, latency, cost and computational load. This paper presents a tiny machine learning (TinyML) pipeline that classifies hand and arm gestures from envelope EMG on a low-cost microcontroller. Four-channel envelope EMG was recorded with a six-lead myoelectric module and an Arduino UNO from 10 healthy participants, who performed six gestures for 4 s each in two sessions. A joint accuracy-complexity search selected the window length, overlap and four time-domain features used to train an artificial neural network (ANN). On a 60/20/20 window-level training/validation/test split, the test accuracy was 98.35%. Five-fold cross-validation (97.37 ± 1.05%) indicated stable performance across data partitions, and leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) evaluation, the only subject-independent test, gave 97.22 ± 1.33%. Compared with a support vector machine (SVM), k-nearest neighbours (KNN), a decision tree and a random forest, the ANN had the lowest golden distance (GD = 0.0325). Deployed on a Raspberry Pi Pico in TensorFlow Lite format, the model uses 9.1% of flash memory and an estimated 10.6% of static random-access memory (SRAM), with a 23 ms inference time, a 254 ms total on-device cycle and a 12.9% active processing duty cycle. In a representative real-time test, with a PC relaying the EMG data to the Pico, per-gesture accuracy over 500 consecutive predictions was 95.8–99.6%. These results show that real-time envelope-EMG gesture recognition is feasible on a resource-constrained microcontroller; with validation on larger and more diverse populations, the approach may inform human-machine interfaces for prosthetics, rehabilitation and assistive devices.

candidates.title: Speaking for Others: A Scoping Review of Entity-Representing Conversational Agents and Interactional Representation
candidates.abstract: Conversational agents increasingly communicate from positions associated with organisations, people, cultural artefacts, and more-than-human entities. However, research on these systems remains fragmented across domains, and it remains unclear how an agent’s interaction becomes a form of representation. We introduce entity-representing conversational agents (ERCAs) as a cross-domain lens for examining this relationship. Through a scoping review of 68 studies across HCI and related fields, with 46 providing the primary evidence for interactional synthesis, we examine how externally anchored agents enact representation through interaction. The retrieved corpus was concentrated in commercial and institutional applications, while personal-proxy, cultural, and more-than-human cases made questions of speaking position, authorisation, and grounding more explicit. Across the studies, representation emerged through the agent’s communicative conduct, its position relative to the represented entity, and users’ interpretations of that relationship. We identify three design considerations for ERCAs: establishing a credible basis for representation, aligning the representative relationship with the entity and task, and sustaining that position through interaction.

candidates.title: Co-Creative Storytelling with a Social Robot: A Pilot Study of Creativity Support
candidates.abstract: This study presents an AI storytelling robot designed to support children’s creativity through collaborative storytelling. The system integrates the communication robot Sota with a Large Language Model (LLM), enabling users to create stories through natural spoken interaction. As an initial feasibility evaluation prior to a study with children, we conducted a pilot study with eight university students. Participants either collaborated with the robot or created stories individually. Creativity was evaluated using a story-rating rubric adapted from four creativity dimensions: fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration, together with a self-report questionnaire. The robot-assisted group showed significantly higher fluency and elaboration scores in the story evaluation, while no significant differences were found in flexibility or originality. No significant group differences were found in the questionnaire results. These preliminary findings suggest that a robot-mediated collaborative storytelling may support idea generation and richer narrative development.
