candidates.title: Device Design for Natural Human-Robot Interaction in Collecting Demonstration Data for Robot Learning
candidates.abstract: Good manipulation learning depends on recording the right data signals. The human hand is guided not just by where it is in space, but by where it touches an object and how hard it is pressing, yet most demonstration systems capture only motion and camera data, leaving out the contact and force information that often matters most. Worse, the recording hardware itself frequently gets in the way, changing how a person naturally handles an object. This thesis describes the hardware and data-collection infrastructure we built toward natural, tactile-rich demonstration, as part of a broader effort on intent-aware robot learning in visually occluded settings. Three things came out of it. First, we analysed an open-source tendon-driven hand and developed a kinematic and tendon-transmission model, which led to two mechanical fixes: a chamfered winch that stopped the tendon from slipping and a thicker, double-jointed coupling link that stopped the fingers from breaking. Both worked, though extended use made clear the platform itself is too fragile to build on, and we document what a successor hand needs to avoid. Second, we built a low-cost glove with force-sensitive resistors on both sides of the hand, with a calibration model and a pipeline that merges the contact data with motion-capture data from a Rokoko glove. Third, I designed a wireless LED band that sits on the robot’s last joint and shows the operator which control mode is active,the mode sleeve,and ran a small user study comparing it against a screen-only baseline. Experienced operators preferred having the sleeve; it let them keep their eyes on the end-effector rather than glancing at the screen, though the benefit depended on having already learned the colour encoding. Together these three components form a toolchain for collecting demonstrations naturally, and for transitioning from human demonstration to autonomous execution with teleoperated fine-tuning.

candidates.title: Using a Social Robot to Promote Interaction Among Older Adults at a Day Center in Japan: a Pilot Study Based on Sociograms
candidates.abstract: This pilot study examines whether the introduction of a social robot can enhance social interaction among older adults attending a day care center in Japan. A quasi-experimental within-subject design with repeated measures was implemented across four group sessions held over one month: one baseline ses-sion without the robot and three sessions with the robot. Using structured observation, sociomatrices, and sociograms, the study analyzed human-human, human-robot, and human-robot-human interaction episodes during guided group activities. Network indicators such as in-degree, out-degree, mean degree, close-ness, betweenness centrality, and authority were compared across sessions to assess changes in relational structure. Brief descriptive interpretation was also complemented by field notes and post-session user evaluations. The baseline ses-sion showed a low-density network with a small active core and several peripheral participants. After the robot was introduced, the volume of exchanges increased and the networks became more cohesive, with higher mean degree values and shorter relational distances. Overall, the findings suggest that the robot func-tioned not only as an object of direct interaction but also as a mediator that stimulated human-robot-human dynamics and helped activate less connected members of the group. Despite these promising results, the study should be inter-preted cautiously due to its pilot nature, small sample, and single-site design. The findings support the potential of social robots as facilitators of group engage-ment in adult day care settings and highlight the usefulness of social network analysis for examining interactional change in gerontechnology research.

candidates.title: User Evaluations and Behavioral Intentions Following Errors by Companion Robots : Effects of Error Severity, Physical Cuteness, and Apology Type
candidates.abstract: 모든 로봇은 완벽하지 않기 때문에 크고 작은 오류는 피할 수 없다. 향후 가정에서 반려 로봇의 입양이 현실화되면 로봇의 오류를 방지하는 것뿐 아니라 오류 이후 손상된 이미지를 완화하는 전략에 대한 고민이 필요하다. 본 연구는 반려 로봇의 오류 발생 이후 이용자의 반응이 오류의 심각성 고저, 로봇의 외형적 귀여움 및 사과 유형에 따라 달라지는지 살펴보았다. 이에 이용자가 사회적 단서를 지닌 로봇을 사회적 행위자로 대한다는 CASA 패러다임에 근거하여, 로봇의 외형적 귀여움은 베이비 스키마를, 사과 유형은 공손 이론을 바탕으로 오류 이후 평가에 작용하는 사회적 단서로 설정하였다. 로봇의 외형, 오류 심각성 및 사과 유형을 조작한 2×2×2 온라인 실험을 성인 640명을 대상으로 실시하였다. 오류 전과 후의 이용자 평가를 분석한 결과, 로봇의 오류 후 이용자의 로봇에 대한 유능함, 따뜻함 인식 및 신뢰는 오류 이전보다 모두 낮아졌다. 특히 심각한 오류는 경미한 오류에 비해 로봇에 대한 평가를 더 크게 훼손하고 용서 의도를 낮추며 사용 중단 의도를 높이는 것으로 나타났다. 반면, 외형과 사과 유형의 효과는 평가 차원에 따라 다르게 나타났다. 귀여운 로봇은 오류 전후에 상대적으로 따뜻하게 평가되었지만, 귀여운 외형이 오류로 인한 평가 손상을 전반적으로 완충하지는 않았다. 또한 귀여운 사과는 오류 이후 따뜻함의 감소를 완화한 반면, 신뢰의 감소폭은 오히려 사무적 사과 조건에서 상대적으로 작게 나타났다. 그러나 두 사과 방식은 용서 의도와 사용 중단 의도에서 뚜렷한 차이를 만들지 않았다. 이러한 결과는 반려 로봇의 오류 심각성이 전반적인 이용자 반응을 결정하는 가운데, 로봇의 외형과 사과 방식은 따뜻함과 신뢰 등 서로 다른 평가 차원에 선택적으로 작용함을 보여준다. 본 연구는 반려 로봇의 오류 완화 전략을 설계할 때 친근한 사회적 단서를 일률적으로 강화하기보다, 회복하고자 하는 평가 차원과 오류의 심각성을 함께 고려해야 함을 시사한다.

candidates.title: HUMAN ROBOT COLLABORATION AND AI-ENABLED WAREHOUSE SAFETY MANAGEMENT FOR SUSTAINABLE LOGISTICS OPERATIONS IN SAUDI ARABIA
candidates.abstract: Robotic warehousing offers opportunities to reduce hazardous manual transport while introducing new risks at shared workstations, aisle intersections and digitally coordinated handovers. This critical integrative review evaluates how human-robot collaboration and artificial intelligence can support safer, more sustainable logistics operations, with Saudi Arabia as the proposed implementation context. Thirty DOI - indexed publications dated 2020 - 2025 were purposively examined across operational research, ergonomics, robotics, occupational safety and logistics management. Evidence was organised around exposure pathways, collaborative task allocation, predictive sensing, safety assurance, workforce acceptance and organisational governance. The synthesis shows that robotics may reduce walking and handling demands, but operational benefits cannot be equated with verified injury reduction. Adaptive speed control, transparent intention signalling, fatigue - aware scheduling and human - centred training appear promising when embedded within independently validated safeguards. Conversely, sensor uncertainty, deadline pressure, opaque algorithmic decisions and fragmented system ownership may transfer rather than remove risk.

candidates.title: Network-Exposed Configuration Attacks on LLM-Controlled Social Robots
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) in embodied robots create security dependencies beyond inference. We investigate a network-exposed configuration attack on the Pollen Robotics Reachy Mini Lite, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to replace personality settings and the cloud LLM's system prompt through a management interface, without adversarial conversational input. Eleven prompt-injection attempts across five categories were reported as resisted, whereas both configuration-layer attack paths produced observable behavioural changes on physical hardware. We demonstrate local and network-adjacent access, mapping the weakness to CWE-306 (Missing Authentication for a Critical Function) and CWE-1327 (Binding to an Unrestricted IP Address), with a reported CVSS v3.1 score of 6.5 (Medium). A configuration endpoint also accepts cross-origin requests without a CORS preflight (CWE-352; 6.5 Medium), while the persistent-memory sink stores content without enforcing its stated restrictions. A source review of 59 public repositories identifies missing authentication in 10 of 11 source-verifiable genuine applications, or 11 of 11 including a framework-default case. These findings indicate recurrence within the sampled repositories, not prevalence in commercial products. We characterise a deployment gap between developer-oriented network assumptions and consumer-facing embodied AI security: inference-layer refusal cannot prevent unauthorised changes to model instructions. Potential consequences include surveillance through onboard cameras and microphones and social engineering of nearby users. Proof-of-concept code, evidence and the survey are available at https://bit.ly/reachypi.

candidates.title: Multimodal Emotion Expression for Android Robot Heads
candidates.abstract: Emotional expression is often treated as a key requirement for social robots: when a robot’s voice, face, and behavior express the same affective state, the interaction becomes more natural, believable, and engaging. However, expressing emotions congruently across multiple modalities, is not trivial, when additional constraints, like a specifically designed voice or lip-synced facial animation, need to be respected at the same time. To tackle this problem we show how zero-shot emotional text-to-speech can be combined with emotion-aware speech-driven facial animation, to make an android robot express affect while preserving a voice previously designed to match its appearance. A user study evaluating the robot’s voice reveals mixed results for different emotions, highlighting the need for multimodal expressions and further investigation.

candidates.title: Impact of restaurant robot service consumption values on their consequences: the moderating effects of perceived risk and human–robot interaction quality
candidates.abstract: Purpose This study examined the effects of consumption values on customers' behavioral intentions toward robot service restaurants, based on the theory of consumption values and the value attitude behavior model. It also analyzed the moderating effects of perceived risk and human–robot interaction quality. Design/methodology/approach The study collected data from 756 customers who experienced robot services in restaurants. A structural equation modeling (SEM) analysis with a multi-group approach was used to test relationships. Findings The results showed that functional, human-like capability, social, emotional and epistemic values significantly predicted attitudes toward robot services, while price, safety and privacy did not. Most consumption values also influenced perceived brand equity, which strongly affected all outcomes including customers' intention to pay more, loyalty, intention to recommend and participation in value co-creation. Perceived risk and human–robot interaction quality partially influenced relationships in the structural model. Research limitations/implications This study has contributed to the literature on consumption value theory by incorporating a new construct – human-like capability – and emphasizing price value and safety and privacy values in the context of robot-provided restaurant services. However, future studies could examine robotic consumption values across a broader range of robot-assisted hospitality and tourism sectors. Practical implications This study provided valuable insights for restaurant managers by identifying robot service consumption values that significantly influence customers' behavioral intentions. Additionally, it demonstrates that service robots enhance service providers' performance through improved service efficiency. Originality/value This study is one of the first to explore robot-induced consumption values based on the responses of actual users of robot services in restaurants, providing findings drawn from customers' practical experiences.

candidates.title: Towards inclusive education mediated by social robotics: trainee educators' perceptions of robotic systems analysis
candidates.abstract: Among the transformations shaping contemporary educational contexts, social robotics is emerging as an innovative technological field capable of introducing physical presence, communication dynamics and multimodal forms of interaction (Neumann, 2023). Unlike other digital technologies, social robots not only perform functions related to instructional support, communication facilitation and adaptive learning (Woo et al., 2021; Youssef et al., 2023), but provided that the intended educational objectives are clearly defined they can also directly influence the emotional and relational dimensions of the educational experience (Martinez-Roig, 2024), affecting interaction patterns, student participation (Woo et al., 2021), motivation and support throughout learning activities (Youssef et al., 2023). In this regard, the use of social robots in educational settings does not automatically lead to improved student learning outcomes. Rather, their effectiveness depends closely on the quality of the learning experience they help create, the role assigned to robotics within educational activities and the extent to which educators and teachers understand and interpret both the opportunities and limitations of social robotics (Mullick, 2025). Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 56-59. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Social Robotics and Socio-Emotional Inclusion.

candidates.title: Distance Does Not Matter: The Role of Physical Robot Presence in Social HRI with Older Adults
candidates.abstract: As the global older population increases, more older adults need assistance in their daily lives. There is an increasing interest in using social robots to assist with everyday activities to promote overall wellbeing and health. However, whether and how social robot physical presence can influence human-robot interactions (HRI) with older adults has not yet been explored. In this paper, we present the first long-term HRI study conducted in a long-term care home that investigates the interaction behaviors of older adults during dance sessions facilitated by physically present and remotely present social human-like robots. Our results show that the older adults had similarly high levels of engagement and enjoyment during the interactions regardless of if the social robot was physically or remotely present. Although higher participation rates were observed in the in-person HRI, participation rates in the remote HRI were consistent to those in other non-robot facilitated physical activity interventions for older adults. Overall, this paper explores the role of robot presence and its impact on HRI, while providing insight into the potential use of remote HRI for providing social assistance to older adults.

candidates.title: Interprofessional and agile development of Mobirobot: a socially assistive robot for paediatric therapy across clinical and therapeutic settings
candidates.abstract: Introduction Socially assistive robots hold promise for supporting paediatric therapy, but adapting them to healthcare practice requires attention to therapeutic goals, professional responsibilities, and local workflows. Using Mobirobot as a case, this paper examines how an interprofessional development process was organised across inpatient sports therapy, inpatient physiotherapy, and outpatient physiotherapy, and how stakeholder input from these settings was translated into changes to the robot and its use. Methods We describe Phase 2 of the Mobirobot project, which ran from 2022 to 2024. Development involved recurring interdisciplinary meetings, weekly technical development meetings, setting-specific exchanges, a care-staff workshop, and testing during visits to the deployment settings. We reviewed 25 meeting and workshop records, which also documented observations from site visits and system changes, to trace selected stakeholder input and development responses. Results The development process produced changes to the robot’s interaction, exercise programme, technical setup, and deployment procedures. Examples include introducing therapist-configurable exercise regimens, adapting robot placement to bedside physiotherapy, discontinuing unreliable heart-rate monitoring, and providing training and troubleshooting support for staff. We draw development lessons from these documented decisions concerning interaction, therapeutic adaptability, professional control, technical robustness, and integration into local practice. Discussion The Mobirobot case illustrates how repeated contact between technical and clinical stakeholders, combined with testing in the intended settings, brought practical stakeholder input into successive development cycles. The records do not establish how frequently needs were expressed or whether the resulting changes improved clinical outcomes. Conclusion Mobirobot provides a longitudinal account of interprofessional robot co-development across three paediatric therapeutic settings. Its development lessons offer considerations for similar projects.

candidates.title: EvoMisty: Building, Optimizing, and Evolving Capabilities on a Social Robot
candidates.abstract: Social robots face diverse and changing tasks in companionship and education. LLM-based methods can generate task programs, but they still rely on manually developed control interfaces and predefined capabilities. They also lack a general mechanism to optimize completed tasks based on user-specified metrics and reuse performance improvements across tasks.We present EvoMisty, a plugin-based framework that enables coding agents to build and continually improve robot capabilities. EvoMisty builds a control program from official documentation and verifies candidate capabilities on a physical robot. Verified capabilities are stored in an atomic capability library and combined with existing skills to solve tasks. After task completion, EvoMisty can collect execution data, measure user-specified metrics, and iteratively improve task programs. It then distills reusable skills from final solutions into a skill library for future tasks.We evaluate EvoMisty on a physical Misty II robot using Claude Code and Codex. The two agents construct 109 and 107 verified atomic capabilities, respectively. Both complete all 28 AutoMisty benchmark tasks and seven additional tasks beyond AutoMisty's capabilities. Optimization improves all seven evaluated metrics across five tasks. For example, dialogue response latency decreases by 52% and 71%, respectively. Reusing skills from one optimized dialogue task reduces latency by 33% to 72% in three other dialogue tasks without further optimization. All code and experimental videos will be publicly released through the webpage: https://wangxiaoshawn.github.io/projects/evomisty/index.html

candidates.title: Working With Robots: How Robot Proportion in Human-Robot Teams and Robot Anthropomorphism Shape Employee Turnover Intention
candidates.abstract: Although robots are increasingly reshaping organizational workflows, how the robot proportion in human-robot teams affects employees’ turnover intention remains underexplored. Drawing on conservation of resources theory, we examine whether, why, and when robot proportion exerts divergent effects on turnover intention through two pathways: resource gain and resource loss. Evidence from a scenario-based experiment (Study 1, N = 290) and a three-wave field study (Study 2, N = 306) reveals that these two pathways operate in opposing directions. Specifically, work goal progress and work loneliness mediate the relationship between robot proportion in human-robot teams and turnover intention. Robot anthropomorphism further moderates these pathways: higher anthropomorphism strengthens the beneficial effect on work goal progress, whereas lower anthropomorphism amplifies the detrimental effect on work loneliness. This study offers initial evidence on how the structural composition of human-robot teams shapes employees’ turnover intention, and it provides practical implications for organizations deploying robotic coworkers.

candidates.title: Human–AI symbiosis and the ethics of care: Towards care-sensitive design in assistive robotics
candidates.abstract: This article examines the ethical challenges raised by assistive robots from the perspective of human-AI symbiosis and the ethics of care.While dominant approaches in AI ethics and machine ethics often rely on principle-based frameworks, we argue that these are insufficient when robotic systems intervene in fragile, embodied, gendered, and asymmetrical relations of care.After reconstructing human-AI symbiosis as a condition of technological co-dependence and vulnerability, the article introduces care ethics as a framework capable of foregrounding dependency, relationality, bodily exposure, contextual responsiveness, and dignity.It then discusses Dyoub and Lisi's fuzzy-logic approach to the Patient Dilemma, showing how their model mediates between autonomy, beneficence, and nonmaleficence in assistive robotics.Building on this case, the article proposes a care-ethical reframing of intimate robotic care through the scenario of incontinence management.This scenario makes visible several intertwined vulnerabilities that are relevant.Finelly, we argue that care-sensitive design should include granular consent, privacy-and dignity-preserving operation, adaptive interaction, human handover, bias audits, inclusive datasets, and participatory design.The aim is to support robotic care without intensifying exposure, dependency, misrecognition, or loss of dignity.

candidates.title: Separating Fiction From Reality: Predictors of Parasocial Relationships With Animated Characters Across Relationship Status
candidates.abstract: Parasocial relationships (PSRs) are one‐sided relationships where an individual has an interest in developing a relationship with another person (the target), but the target is unaware of the actor's existence. The goal of the present research was to understand whether a participant having a PSR relates to potential deficits in their social or romantic needs. Anime fans, both single and in human‐human romantic relationships, were surveyed to assess factors associated with seeking out PSRs with fictional characters. We found an association between loneliness and having a PSR, but no association between psychological well‐being and having a PSR. We also found evidence for a partial mediation wherein having a PSR is associated with lower psychological well‐being scores. We did not find any association between relationship deficits and having a PSR. These findings suggest that people may develop PSRs due to wanting more social connections, but not due to physical or emotional deficits in one's romantic relationships.

candidates.title: Talk to Act: A Synthetic Multi-Turn Dialogue Benchmark for Human Intent Extraction and Action Planning in Robotics
candidates.abstract: Multi-turn conversational human-robot interaction (HRI) continues to be a challenging problem in robotics, as many existing systems rely on rigid, command-driven interfaces that can be unintuitive for users. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) provide a promising direction, given their ability to process natural language, generate structured outputs, and support tool-based reasoning, all of which are relevant for interpreting user intent in robotic settings. However, progress in this area is constrained by the limited availability of datasets and benchmarks that capture the nuances of real-world human communication, such as multi-turn dialogue, ambiguity, and context-dependent requests. In this work, we present a synthetically generated multi-turn dialogue dataset for HRI, annotated with action intents, object references, and task plans across a range of scenarios and user personas. Our primary focus is on evaluating the capability of small, open-weight language models for robotic tasks, particularly in settings where local deployment and efficiency are important. To this end, we frame intent extraction as a tool-calling problem where each predicted action corresponds to a structured function call with arguments grounded in the dialogue and benchmark models ranging from 270M to 8B parameters on their ability to perform intent extraction and action planning without task-specific fine-tuning. Our results show that these models can achieve reasonable performance on the task even at relatively small scales and without any task-specific fine-tuning. This suggests that compact, locally deployable models already provide a useful baseline for conversational robotic systems. We expect that task-specific fine-tuning and more realistic training data will enhance performance further and make such models increasingly suitable for real-world robotic applications.

candidates.title: “Cute Companion” or “Awful Thing”: Understanding Individual Differences in Attitudes to Social Robots as Pets
candidates.abstract: For users unable to keep pets due to logistical, financial, or health reasons, social robots could offer a substitute. However, these robots remain uncommon in domestic use, and it is unclear how individual user traits or robot attributes impact receptivity or perceptions toward social robots as pets. We conducted a mixed-methods survey exploration (N = 163) of respondents' initial receptivity and preconceptions regarding five robots with varied morphologies to understand whether these perceptions correlated with individual traits. We found that indi-vidual differences in anthropomorphism propensity, pet attachment and lower age all predicted positive initial perceptions of the social robots as domestic com-panions, guiding future expectations. Furthermore, a divide emerged between participants with non-negotiable philosophical objections to robot pets and those with addressable concerns around robot fidelity and agency. We discuss the impli-cations of user perceptions on the current feasibility of domestic robot pets and provide actionable directions for robot development. Supplementary Information: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s12369-026-01453-4.

candidates.title: Towards Multilingual End-of-Turn Detection using Frozen Speech Encoders
candidates.abstract: A spoken dialogue system must judge when the user has yielded the floor. This end-of-turn (EoT) detector is normally trained and tuned afresh for each language, which is costly to scale to new languages. We instead build one on a frozen multilingual encoder, training only a small fixed-size head. Using five CALLHOME languages, we investigate three questions. First, how well a head trained on one language transfers zero-shot to the others. Second, how much target-language adaptation is required to recover full task performance. Third, whether a single fixed decision threshold holds across languages without per-language tuning. We find that the head transfers well, even between tonal and pitch-accent languages, and that a few hours of audio recover nearly all the loss, matching in-language training. A frozen multilingual encoder with one lightweight head is a practical, language-agnostic baseline for EoT detection.

candidates.title: Emo-H2A: Driving a Facial Robot Directly from LLM Hidden States at Token Rate
candidates.abstract: Diverse, semantically synchronized, and low-latency facial expressions are essential for human-robot interaction. While large language models (LLMs) have endowed anthropomorphic robots with fluent speech, facial expression still struggles to follow the conversation. Motivated by this gap, we present Emo-H2A (hidden-to-actuation), a paradigm that drives a facial robot directly from LLM hidden states during autoregressive decoding. Without a separate emotion label, expression stays continuous and context-sensitive, and the face moves with the unfolding reply. We instantiate this paradigm as EmoManifold, a training-free method that extracts a valence-arousal-dominance (VAD) coordinate from each hidden state, projects it, and drives the face at token granularity. The readout is checked on six language models, and the same projection drives our 29-degree-of-freedom (DoF) facial robot. When driven by this projection, the face shifts its expression in the matching direction on 87.5% of within-reply valence transitions, whereas holding a single label for the whole reply leaves directional tracking near the 50% chance level, and first moves in 0.96s rather than waiting 10-26s for the reply to finish and a turn-level label to return.

candidates.title: Just Between Us? Exploring a Wearable-Mediated Channel for Discreet Human-Agent Interaction in a Shared Game Setting
candidates.abstract: In shared settings, social robots may need to exchange information with an individual while limiting co-present others' access to or interpretation of that information. Publicly observable speech and gestures may not adequately support such exchanges. We investigate a wearable-mediated channel for discreet interaction that combines in-ear audio messages with deliberate rightward head tilts as responses. To examine its feasibility and participants' experiences, we studied 20 pairs (40 participants) playing a card game with a screen-based conversational agent representing a social robot, controlled by a researcher in a Wizard-of-Oz setup. Each pair played with and without the channel. One participant wore the device (the wearer), while the other (the non-wearer) was informed about the channel after gameplay. The channel conveyed information that could help the wearer or robot character select an opponent they could defeat. The information exchange and subsequent opponent selection occurred as intended in 39 of 40 channel-mediated turns. Wearers reported low perceived pressure/tension in both conditions, with no statistically significant difference between conditions, and favorable usability immediately after use. Retrospective interviews, however, revealed varied accounts of noticing the interaction among non-wearers and contrasting perceptions of teamwork and unfairness. These findings support the feasibility of wearable-mediated exchanges within this game and identify awareness and fairness as considerations for future designs.

candidates.title: From Discipline to Studio: Creative Practice and a Transdisciplinary Turn in Social Robotics
The prosocial robot navigation charter: a framework based on normative cards
candidates.abstract: Recently, the social robotics community established a set of principles for social robot navigation, including safety, comfort, legibility, politeness, social norms, agent understanding, proactivity, and contextual awareness. These principles were developed to guide the design of algorithms that achieve social behavior implicitly, but recent advances enable guiding behavior explicitly with language instructions supplied to large language models. Furthermore, robotics foundation models enable zero-shot execution of open-set tasks while remaining safe for users, using techniques like visual-language understanding, grounded action models, and constitutional safety systems. These new features suggest an opportunity to use the social robot navigation principles as a constitution for social behavior for a language-based agent. Furthermore, these new capabilities suggest expanding the social navigation principles to support more sophisticated behaviors. Since language-based agents are capable of understanding their relationship to their users, nearby pedestrians, and the community, we argue that the next generation of socially navigating robots should be prosocial: that is, actively trying to improve the social navigation environment they operate in. This requires not merely being good pedestrians in the navigation environment, but good participants in the social environment—taking on tasks such as clearing obstructions, alerting others to hazards, and giving directions to passersby, as long as these tasks are within the robot’s capabilities and do not interfere with the robot’s goals. This paper reviews the social navigation principles, argues for a definition of prosocial robot navigation, and explores how literate artificial intelligence can use the research literature itself to guide agents. To ensure the resulting guidance is aligned with human expectations, the paper proposes a Normative Card Architecture which specifies how robots ought to behave in terms of schema-verifiable, machine-auditable, human-approved, automatically-assembled machine-readable charters for robotics agents that use language-model planning. The paper then describes a Prosocial Navigation Charter which implements the prosocial navigation principles in the Normative Card Architecture framework, and presents a proof-of-concept demonstration of the framework’s support for auditability.

candidates.title: Comparing a tutor and peer-learner social robot in a vocabulary learning activity
candidates.abstract: The purpose of this study is to compare two different roles for a social robot to assume in a robot-assisted learning activity. Study participants learned 12 vocabulary words in Esperanto with either a robot assuming a tutor role, or a peer-learner role. Results found that participants’ general attitudes and perceptions towards both robot roles were positive. Usability scores were high in both conditions, mostly positive user experiences in were reported both conditions. While there was no significant difference in learning outcomes between conditions, participants in the peer-learner condition completed the post-lesson quiz 30% faster, which could indicate more meaningful learning occurred and suggest that interaction and instructional characteristics associated with peer learning, such as increased engagement, confidence, or retrieval practice, contributed to this difference. A thematic analysis of participants’ responses to open-ended questions shows participants’ opinions on the system in both conditions, including a desire for more interaction with the peer-learner robot, feeling that the robot provides companionship and is interactive, feeling comfortable and not-judged by the robot, and envisioning real-life applications of such learning system. Findings from the thematic analysis also provide directions for future research and technology development for Robot-Assisted Language Learning (RALL).

candidates.title: Teachy mini: a knowledge-based generative social robot for responsible tutoring in higher education
candidates.abstract: Introduction Generative social robots (GSRs) powered by large language models offer new possibilities for personalized tutoring in higher education, but also introduce risks related to misinformation, missing transparency, or reinforcing incorrect student responses. Prior work identified knowledge-based design (KBD) requirements that define the information GSRs need to tutor responsibly and effectively in higher education. Methods In this paper, we operationalized selected KBD requirements in the Reachy Mini robot platform through system prompting, retrieval-augmented generation, and stateful prompt orchestration. We present Teachy Mini, a GSR tutoring prototype based on these design requirements. To test the system, we conducted a preliminary evaluation study. Participants (N = 24) completed a robot-guided learning session about research methodologies. They learned with either Teachy Mini or a robot without the KBD features. Results and discussion Teachy Mini was perceived as significantly more aligned with responsible tutoring behavior than the robot in the control condition. In addition, a qualitative analysis showed that Teachy Mini more often used context-sensitive explanations, Socratic questions, and personalized feedback compared to the robot without KBD features. No significant between-condition differences were found in system acceptance, intrinsic motivation, or learning effectiveness, although exploratory analyses suggested a positive effect of KBD on objective learning gains when accounting for learner preferences. Furthermore, an exploratory path model suggested that the robot’s perceived responsible behavior may be associated with learner motivation and acceptance. Overall, the study suggests that KBD can meaningfully shape responsible robot tutoring behavior. However, the effect of KBD on learner experiences requires further research.

candidates.title: The New Housemates: Framing Social Robots as Cohabitants of Independent Ageing
candidates.abstract: This paper reports on a qualitative, design-led case study with eleven independently living older Australians who imagined how social robots might enter their homes, routines and futures. Through asynchronous design activities, interviews, provotype development and a co-design workshop using a provotype, we examined how participants imagined social robots as part of independent living at home. Findings show that expectations for robots were shaped by three interconnected domains: ageing through contribution and adaptation, home as a carefully curated environment and robots as conditional cohabitants for ageing independently. Rather than replacing existing ecology of ageing design guidance, we show how ecological fit becomes more complex when technologies are communicative, adaptive and potentially co-present in the home. We propose the housemate as a critical framing for social robot design in independent living contexts: a conditional domestic presence that must be useful, respectful of boundaries and adaptable without taking over.

candidates.title: Systematic review of the use of programmable and social robots in mathemathics education and its link to educational inclusion
candidates.abstract: This article presents a systematic review on the use of robots in mathematics teaching, with an emphasis on educational inclusion. Forty-two studies selected from the Scopus and Web of Science databases were analysed using the PRISMA method, identifying that 85.7% use programmable robots such as BeeBot, 14.3% use social robots such as NAO and Pepper, and the majority of the research is concentrated in Spain, Italy, South Korea, and the United States. Robots are mainly used to foster computational thinking, problem solving and educational inclusion. 40.4% of the studies address inclusion, showing significant improvements in mathematics learning and student motivation. The findings position educational robotics as an innovative tool for inclusive teaching and the promotion of active and motivating pedagogical practices.

candidates.title: Decoding anthropomorphism: a multidimensional perspective on presence, parasocial relationship and purchase intention
candidates.abstract: Virtual influencers have become an increasingly important marketing tool, yet existing research has offered limited insight into how their anthropomorphic attributes should be conceptualized and through which psychological mechanisms they influence consumer responses. Addressing this gap, this study conceptualizes virtual influencer anthropomorphism as a multidimensional construct consisting of physical anthropomorphism, interactivity intelligence, and mental human-likeness, and examines its effects on purchase intention through social presence, telepresence, and parasocial relationship. Using online survey data, the results show that all three anthropomorphic attributes positively enhance consumers’ social presence and telepresence, which in turn strengthen parasocial relationships and subsequently increase purchase intention. The findings further refine the conceptualization of virtual influencer anthropomorphism by highlighting the importance of interaction-based anthropomorphism alongside visual and mental human-like cues. Overall, this study contributes to the literature by clarifying both the multidimensional nature of virtual influencer anthropomorphism and the psychological process through which it shapes consumer behavior.

candidates.title: Emotions and anthropomorphism towards robots: a scoping review
candidates.abstract: Human interaction with non-human entities, such as robots, has long been characterised by anthropomorphism – namely, the tendency to attribute human-like mental states to inanimate objects. While humans appear evolutionarily hardwired to use anthropomorphism as the default strategy for navigating interactions with their peers, significant gaps remain in the Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) field in defining and operationalising “emotions” and their relationship to psychological anthropomorphism towards robots. This scoping review aims to systematically map the existing HRI literature and see how emotions are investigated in relation to robots. By reviewing relevant empirical studies, it addresses four core research questions focusing on: (i) the conceptualisation of emotions and anthropomorphism towards robots; (ii) prevailing theoretical models and definitions; (iii) methodologies used to investigate emotions in HRI; and (iv) key findings in the literature regarding the emotions-anthropomorphism link. This review contributes to broaden current discussions about how emotions are conceptualised and analysed in HRI research, by which it would be possible to contribute to extend knowledge about how people emotionally interact with robots by considering their anthropomorphism.

candidates.title: Learned lessons on Socially Assistive Robot design in Elderly Care: proposal and insights of a Collaborative Design Framework
candidates.abstract: Purpose: This paper proposes a co-design framework and evaluates its practical application during a project involving robot deployment in a retirement home.Methods: The study details the hybrid methodology used during a 19-week Socially Assistive Robot deployment involving 17 older adults and 3 professionals in a Spanish retirement home. Robot performance was evaluated via the AUSUS framework, prioritizing techniques designed to minimize participant fatigue.Results: While participants reported high perceived utility, the deployment revealed two distinct obstacles. First, low technical efficacy was primarily driven by inherent unpredictability and daily incidents of a real-world environment, which negatively cascaded into the overall user experience. Second, the study exposed the inherent limitations of traditional User-Centered Design practices, particularly the challenge of defining and sustaining active participant engagement within complex, shared care ecosystems. Conclusion: Driven by the lessons learned from the CAMPERO project, the paper underscores the necessity for contextual pre-assessments, active participant empowerment, and pragmatic evaluation scoping. Ultimately, these insights provide a critical foundation for future methodological advancements, ensuring SAR deployments are genuinely collaborative, needs-driven, methodologically responsible and integrated without disrupting the care ecosystem.

candidates.title: GVT3D: Gesture-Vision-Text Token Enrichment for 3D Embodied Reference Understanding
candidates.abstract: Natural human-robot interaction requires robots to interpret language and gestures within a 3D environment to support tasks such as pick-and-place and object retrieval. 3D Embodied Reference Understanding (3D-ERU) supports this by identifying the 3D location of a target object from a scene (point-cloud) containing a human pointing gesture and an accompanying language description. However, current 3D-ERU models lack alignment of cross-modal representations and incur high processing costs that increase with the point-cloud's size. To address this, we propose GVT3D, which employs an Embodied Fusion module that jointly models language, gesture, and vision inputs within a shared embedding space, promoting cross-modal alignment. We additionally introduce a foveation approach that selectively processes the point cloud within a coarse region around the estimated pointing direction to reduce computations. GVT3D achieves ~8% higher accuracy and foveation enables 2.95x faster execution while maintaining comparable accuracy, relative to prior 3D-ERU models.

candidates.title: Human behaviour and intention prediction for industrial human-robot collaboration: Potentials, challenges, and opportunities
candidates.abstract: The behaviour of humans when collaborating with other actors such as other humans or robots has been studied for decades and remains critical for unlocking mixed human-robot team performance. To achieve better, more effective human-robot collaboration (HRC) in industrial settings, a robot needs to have robust models to predict human behaviour when working towards a shared goal. Inferring and modelling human intentions is expected to play a pivotal role in accurately predicting human behaviour as suggested in this paper. This paper explores the potentials, challenges, and opportunities in human behaviour and intention prediction for industrial HRC. It first examines human factors in socio-technical systems, highlighting the challenges of human-human collaboration that inform the design of human-robot teams. Building on this foundation, a human behaviour and intention prediction framework is introduced that enables seamless HRC by integrating behavioural modelling techniques. The paper further reviews perception systems used to interpret the physical world and decode physiological and affective states, along with reasoning and planning strategies based on probabilistic, rule-based, machine learning, hybrid, and language model approaches. Verification and validation methodologies are discussed to ensure reliability and safety, followed by an analysis of the ethical, legal, and societal implications of predictive modelling in industrial HRC. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of open challenges and future research directions, emphasising advancements in adaptive modelling, perception-driven reasoning, and ethical frameworks to shape the next generation of collaborative robots that are robust, human-centric, and ethically responsible. Data Availability No new data were generated or analysed in this study.

candidates.title: VagueBench: Benchmarking the Robustness of Embodied Agents on Ambient Context Illusions
candidates.abstract: Embodied agents are increasingly deployed in open-world environments, yet current robustness evaluations remain biased toward hazardous instructions and jailbreak vulnerabilities. A more fundamental issue is largely overlooked: agents are rarely tested under semantically sufficient but contextually minimal instructions (i.e., common in real-world human communication), where auxiliary contextual cues are absent. For the first, we identify a novel phenomenon termed Ambient Context Illusion, where agents fail to execute tasks correctly when non-essential contextual details are omitted, despite unchanged task semantics. To systematically study this, we establish VagueBench, a benchmark built upon the AI2-THOR interactive simulation environment for the evaluation of context dependency in embodied agents. We systematically consider key semantic components of instructions (entities, procedures, constraints, and prior knowledge) and derive a unified taxonomy with four categories and nine subtypes to reduce auxiliary information. VagueBench contains 1,303 instruction pairs across diverse indoor environments, constructed via a human-agent co-generation framework that integrates semantic redundancy estimation, taxonomy-guided transformation, and rigorous semantic-invariance verification. Through extensive evaluation on 6 state-of-the-art embodied agents, we observe significant degradation on VagueBench in both task performance and executability (relatively -19.65% in task success rate and relatively +54.10% in empty plan rate) revealing a strong reliance on auxiliary linguistic signals rather than core task semantics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this phenomenon persists in real-world robotic systems, where it can lead to incorrect decisions and potential safety risks.

candidates.title: TinyML Hits the Memory Wall: A Benchmark of Ten Sub-Watt Edge Devices
candidates.abstract: Neural network inference at the edge must fit tight energy budgets. Existing benchmarks compare few devices, do not report energy on a common basis, and omit the newest microcontrollers with an NPU or the 1 GHz Cortex-M85. Hardware-aware design also ranks networks by MAC count, yet no study has tested whether this proxy holds across accelerators. We benchmark sub-watt edge AI hardware by evaluating four CNNs (MobileNetV3, MCUNetV1, EfficientNet, SqueezeNet) and two tiny transformers (MobileViT-XXS, DeiT-tiny) on ten commercial devices: an in-sensor DSP (Sony IMX500), four MCUs with an NPU (STM32N6, Alif Ensemble E7/E8, GreenWaves GAP9), and five MCUs without an NPU (STM32U5, Apollo510B, ESP32-S3 Xtensa LX7, RA8M2, STM32V8). Four devices are novel (Alif E8, Apollo510B, RA8M2, STM32V8). Measured as energy above idle, the IMX500 (0.13-0.35 mJ) uses 1.3-3x less energy than the STM32N6 (0.31-1.05 mJ) on every model; the GAP9 uses the least on MobileNetV3 and the Alif E7 the least on MCUNetV1 and SqueezeNet. All four use 6-34x less energy than the STM32V8 (1.85-3.98 mJ), and the Alif E7 and IMX500 form the power-performance Pareto front. Latency on all four accelerators scales with memory traffic (bytes of weights and activations, r >= 0.98) and not with MACs, so they are memory-bound, while no MCU without an NPU is. The NPU advantage grows with intensity from 1.4x over a 1 GHz Cortex-M85 on MCUNetV1 to 8.2x on SqueezeNet. MAC count is therefore a misleading cost proxy for sub-watt accelerators.

candidates.title: A deep learning framework for human motion prediction and biomechanical risk assessment in human-robot collaboration
candidates.abstract: Within the human-centered Industrial 5.0 paradigm, ensuring worker safety and health in human-robot collaboration (HRC) environments constitutes a fundamental operational and ethical priority. Conventional ergonomic risk assessment methodologies are increasingly inadequate for the dynamic, adaptive demands of HRC, because they lack real-time responsiveness, and insufficient predictive capacity. While commercial inertial motion capture systems show accurate joint kinematics, they are not suitable for scalable, proactive risk intervention because of their prohibitive cost, labor-intensive calibration procedures, and architectural reliance on post-hoc computation. To address this gap, this study introduces and validates a deep learning–driven framework for advancing work ergonomics assessment toward both predictive fidelity and field-deployable practicality. The primary contribution is a multi-scale spatiotemporal graph attention network (MS-STGAN). It is designed for forecasting short-term human joint angles from low-cost, wearable inertial measurement unit (IMU) signals. Leveraging a graph-structured representation of the human skeleton and spatiotemporal attention mechanisms, MS-STGAN models the human biomechanical coherence and task-specific temporal patterns inherent in industrial operations. Subsequently, this prediction module is integrated with a physics-informed biomechanical model to construct an end-to-end pipeline, i.e., using raw IMU data to prospective estimation of joint forces and torques. Quantitative evaluation demonstrates that MS-STGAN outperforms the evaluated baseline models in joint angle prediction (RMSE: 2.882°; MAE: 1.888°). The full pipeline enables estimation of joint loading, which exhibits alignment with ground-truth reference data acquired via high-fidelity optical motion capture. In a simulation of an HRC assembly task, the framework enabled risk alerts, confirming its viability for real-time preventive intervention. In short, this work not only delivers a validated, predictive ergonomics assessment architecture but establishes an algorithmic foundation and a clearly articulated development pathway toward affordable, scalable, and anticipatory intelligent ergonomics systems for Industry 5.0.

candidates.title: From Artificial to Humanlike: A Systematic Literature Review of AI Humanisation and Customer Experience
candidates.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) at the customer interface chatbots, voice assistants, virtual agents and service robots is increasingly designed to look, sound and behave like a human being. This review synthesises the evidence on how that deliberate humanisation shapes customer experience (CX), drawing on 57 sources published between 1994 and 2026 across marketing, information systems, hospitality and psychology. Organising the literature through anthropomorphism theory, the Computers-Are-Social-Actors paradigm and the warmth–competence framework, the review examines the design mechanisms through which AI is humanised, the effects of humanisation on trust, engagement, satisfaction and loyalty-relevant behaviour, the boundary conditions that moderate or reverse those effects, and a dark-side literature documenting uncanny-valley discomfort, privacy inference and misplaced trust. The evidence supports a positive but modest and strongly conditional relationship between humanisation and customer evaluations. Humanisation appears to operate by raising customers’ relational expectations of an AI agent: whether its effect is positive or negative depends on whether those expectations can plausibly be met, given the customer’s emotional state, the warmth demanded by the service task, the timing of disclosure and the consequences of failure. Beyond a threshold of human-likeness, and in the presence of privacy concern or perceived deception, the relationship turns negative. The review offers an integrative framework, translates the evidence into heuristics for calibrating humanisation, and identifies gaps in longitudinal, generative-AI and emerging-market evidence.

candidates.title: Robots That Talk Too Much and Don't Listen Enough
candidates.abstract: Until recently, the biggest obstacles to natural spoken interaction with social robots were speech recognition errors and turn-taking failures. Advances in speech recognition have enabled much better spoken interaction, but turn-taking failures and other misunderstandings continue to be far too prevalent. This short paper looks back at earlier methods for improving speech recognition and turn-taking in interaction with social robots, and then looks at what can be done today, arguing that multimodal bidirectional streaming is needed to reduce the frequency of turn-taking failures.

candidates.title: Embodied Multimedia: From Multimedia Content to Situated Human-AI Interaction
candidates.abstract: Multimedia research, which has traditionally been concerned with the analysis and generation of multimedia content, has increasingly addressed multimodal human behavior. This development is exemplified by current ACM Multimedia Challenges, including POLY-SIM [3], which addresses robust speaker identification under missing-modality and cross-lingual scenarios, MultiMediate [2], which targets engagement estimation across domain, age, and culture, and REACT [4], which focuses on generating appropriate facial reactions in dyadic interactions. Together, these challenges reflect a broader shift from analyzing multimedia content toward analyzing, understanding and generating multimodal behavior in increasingly complex social contexts. The next frontier is to develop embodied AI systems that understand, support, and fluently participate in situated human interaction. We pursue this vision through virtual agents and social robots that facilitate communication between people and AI and increasingly between people themselves. The talk will demonstrate how pretrained multimodal foundation models can be leveraged to create context-aware embodied AI. Drawing on applications in assistive communication, AI-mediated group discussions, and social coaching, the talk will illustrate how embodied agents enabled by these models can help overcome communication barriers, facilitate social interaction, and foster authentic self-expression. At the same time, significant challenges remain in grounding multimodal models in physical and social context, ensuring responsive and coordinated behavior, and evaluating whether apparently socially intelligent behavior is appropriate, robust, and trustworthy [1].

candidates.title: CAREFox: An LLM-Assisted Embodied Multimodal Companion for Care-Based EFL Learning with Children
candidates.abstract: This paper presents CAREFox, an LLM-assisted embodied multimodal companion system for supporting children's English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning through care-based interaction. We first conducted a formative study with three child-parent pairs to inform the system design. Based on these insights, CAREFox pairs an embodied robot capable of speech and touch interaction with a vocabulary-selection app, forming a closed-loop multimodal pipeline among child input, companion state, LLM responses, and embodied feedback. Rather than presenting vocabulary practice as an explicit task, CAREFox uses graded hunger and affective states to invite children to feed and interact with the fox through English words and short dialogues. CAREFox demonstrates how LLM-assisted multimodal embodied interaction can support situated vocabulary practice through care based child-robot interaction.

candidates.title: I Believe in You: Robot Identity Design and Service Initiative
candidates.abstract: Some public-service tasks involve requests for personal information, making a robot's presented role and service behavior relevant to users’ privacy perceptions. We examine professional identity cues and service proactivity in a simulated Chinese government-service setting. Semi-structured interviews (\(n=17\)) informed the study design; a pilot study (\(n=34\)) checked the manipulations; and a 2×2 within-subjects virtual study (\(n=36\)) measured self-reported privacy sensitivity and the depth of simulated disclosure. In the main study, participants reported lower privacy sensitivity with robots presented as having a professional identity, and service proactivity interacted with identity presentation. Interviewees differed in their preferences: some found passive service less intrusive, whereas others valued proactive assistance for anticipating their needs. These findings concern perceptions and choices in a simulation, not the robot's actual institutional authorization or data security. They inform context-sensitive interaction design without treating increased disclosure as a goal or professional appearance as proof of privacy protection.

candidates.title: Humanoid Robotics
candidates.abstract: This five-part (in fact, six-part) study did not begin with the ambition of presenting a functioning humanoid robot, nor with the expectation that the proposed architecture could be empirically realised within the scope of this research. Its point of departure was more fundamental: the question of how a future humanoid robot might be organised if cognition is approached not exclusively as computational processing, but as an embodied, temporal, adaptive and physical process. Proceeding from this question, an architectural line of reasoning has been developed across five successive parts. The Human Robot examines the functional and cognitive conditions for an embodied social robot. The DNA Chip as a Neuromorphic Configuration Core introduces a configuration principle by which structural and developmental conditions can be specified. Neuromorphic Hardware Substrate shifts the focus to the physical substrate of these processes. The Vertical Layered Architecture subsequently integrates function, configuration, and hardware into a single reciprocal system structure, while The Physics of Cognition finally asks which physical and temporal principles might underlie such a cognitive organisation. The collective contribution of these parts should therefore not be sought in the empirical confirmation of a single, completed robotic system. Nor is it claimed that all the individual mechanisms are original. Many of the biological, neuroscientific, neuromorphic, and robotic principles on which the architecture builds have their own established research traditions. The intended contribution lies in their architectural coherence: the attempt to treat cognition, memory, learning, temporality, embodiment, configuration, safety, and physical realisation not as separate technical problems, but as interdependent aspects of a single system. Accordingly, this study represents primarily a research proposal. It sets out a route, specifies design principles, and makes explicit where biological inspiration gives way to functional abstraction and where functional abstraction would require technical realisation. It is precisely at this boundary that restraint must be exercised. Biological plausibility does not constitute evidence of technical superiority; a coherent architecture does not in itself demonstrate that the architecture will function stably; and a theoretical advantage in local, event-driven or neuromorphic processing cannot, in the absence of empirical measurement, be translated into a quantified energetic superiority. These limitations do not, however, necessarily diminish the significance of the central research question. Rather, they define its proper scientific status. The architecture proposed here must remain open to confirmation, modification or rejection as future simulations, hardware experiments and humanoid prototypes may warrant. After all, scientific value lies not solely in obtaining confirmation, but also in formulating a problem in such a way that subsequent developments can demonstrate where an assumption holds and where it must be abandoned. This is particularly relevant now that humanoid robotics is developing rapidly. Increasing performance in perception, language, planning, and motor execution demonstrates the power of large-scale learned models and increasingly sophisticated robotic platforms. At the same time, fundamental questions remain concerning continual adaptation, energy consumption, autobiographical memory, intrinsic temporality, embodied meaning-making, local plasticity, and the way safety must be structurally anchored in an autonomous physical system. The development of more powerful models alone does not necessarily render these questions obsolete. The approach proposed here should therefore not be read as an opposition between existing artificial intelligence (AI) and an alternative intended to replace it. A more plausible prospect is that different paradigms will complement one another. Large-scale models may provide powerful semantic and deliberative capabilities, while local neuromorphic processes, fast sensorimotor circuits, adaptive memory systems, and physically anchored safety mechanisms support other timescales and functions. The relevant question then becomes not which paradigm will ultimately ‘win,’ but how these different forms of information processing can be organised within a coherent, energy-efficient, and safe embodied system. This also brings a broader responsibility into view. The aim of humanoid robotics should not be solely to construct a machine that appears ever more human or is able to perform an ever-wider range of human tasks. As such systems become more autonomous and operate in closer proximity to humans and their living environments, it becomes increasingly important to ask how their autonomy is bounded, how they learn, what they remember, how they respond to uncertainty and how safety is incorporated into their physical and cognitive organisation from the outset. The five parts of this study may therefore ultimately be summarised in a single premise: if future humanoid systems are genuinely to function alongside humans over extended periods, cognition, body, learning, memory, temporality, energy consumption, social regulation and safety cannot continue indefinitely to be treated as independent technical sub-problems. Together, they constitute an architectural problem. Whether the answers proposed here will prove to be correct is not something this study can determine. Future research may confirm some principles, replace others, and arrive at solutions not anticipated here. This is not a shortcoming of a conceptual research architecture, but precisely the condition under which it can acquire scientific significance. The ultimate criterion for this study is therefore not whether future humanoid robots will be built precisely according to the architecture described here. A more meaningful criterion is whether the questions posed, the connections drawn and the design principles proposed prove useful in understanding and developing future embodied cognitive systems. Should future developments demonstrate that certain proposals were untenable, the architecture must be revised. Should other principles unexpectedly prove to recur in functioning systems, this would provide a basis for further testing. In either case, the study will have fulfilled its purpose: not by establishing in advance what the humanoid robot of the future will look like, but by offering a coherent and testable framework against which part of that future can be examined. Progress in humanoid robotics is not merely a question of what becomes technically possible. It is equally a question of what form of artificial autonomy we wish to allow to emerge responsibly alongside humans. Against this background, the architecture developed here is intended not as an end point, but as a contribution to a longer scientific trajectory in which technical progress, biological inspiration and human responsibility must remain interconnected.

candidates.title: Editorial: Multimodal human action recognition in real or virtual environments
candidates.abstract: The motivation is to explore cutting-edge research on multimodal human action recognition, focusing on novel methodologies, applications, and future directions in both real and virtual worlds. Integrating AI, robotics, and immersive technologies to improve action understanding and interaction may lead to robotic systems that work alongside humans and interpret and anticipate next movements rather than merely react to them. Also, immersive systems may treat the user's movements as input to a training application, which may recognize both the underlying action and, at the same time, act as a security surveillance system. Similar challenges occur in these settings, where fusing heterogeneous data streams, meeting real-time and hardware limits, coping with scarce or missing data, and evaluating systems based on their effect on humans are measured by different benchmarks.Wearable and physiological sensing in sport and training (Xi et al., 2026) proposed a novel framework for personalized sports health promotion that synchronizes 12-dimensional multimodal data with physiological indicators in real time and applied a transformer graph convolutional network architecture to action recognition. The authors evaluated their framework using a12-week randomized controlled trial, showing that their approach supports accurate motion analysis and safe, personalized intervention. (Cao, 2026) also examined the fusion of kinematic and physiological sequences, using a dual-stream LSTM network with temporal attention applied after each stream has been encoded separately. Vision-based recognition on constrained hardware (Wang et al., 2026) introduced the MA-Pose dataset that consists of 433 videos across 13 martial-arts categories. The authors proposed a dynamic multi-stream, multi-scale graph convolutional network implemented in a multi-stream graph convolutional network that integrates joint, bone, and motion features. The proposed approach achieved moderate classification accuracy while it is feasible to run on a Raspberry Pi 4B, demonstrating that the deployment achieves edge-device feasibility. The authors' honest claim that their development-set results prove that their approach is viable on cutting-edge hardware rather than achieving instantaneous recognition is a candor we welcome.Finally, (Attrah, 2026) studied the facial expression problem and presented a lightweight LSTM that processes facial blendshapes taken directly from a live-streamed camera feed to estimate emotion using the MediaPipe library Face Landmarker task. This approach is restricted to three classes, namely happiness, sadness, or unknown, for embedded systems in social robots. Both papers favor compact and robust models which are well suited to robotic systems and cutting-edge devices achieving maximal accuracy.Virtual environments (Li et al., 2026) addressed an open vulnerability problem that follows from treating motion as a credential. That is, a malicious agent may use a forecasting model generate plausible movements and impersonate a user's behavior in a VR authentication system. The authors trained a fully convolutional network using the 3D position data for the right-hand controller collected using 3 VR systems, namely a Meta Quest, HTC Vive, and HTC Vive Cosmos, to distinguish real and fake hand-controller trajectories, achieving high accuracies in protection against motion forecasting-based attacks in VR authentication systems. (Teng et al., 2025) combined an eye-tracking module and a single-channel EEG module with manual controllers so that users operate two hands and a virtual third limb through integration of Tobii eye-tracking, NeuroSky single-channel EEG, and non-haptic controllers. Their study included eight participants and demonstrated a high virtual hand success rate and reduced spatial error compared to traditional dual-hand control, suggesting that precision in accessible tri-manual VR applications for rehabilitation, training, and assistive technologies is feasible.Finally, (Cordeiro et al., 2025) conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic review that consists of 37 studies from 2021 to 2025. The authors identified the attributes needed to evaluate industrial safety training with immersive technologies in high-risk environments, including the fusion of biometric and behavioral data to infer human actions in real time.These articles showed that multimodal human action recognition may move from sterilized laboratory demonstrations toward systems that are capable of deploying noisy or missing signals, and secure and evaluate against outcomes for different users. candidates.title: From virtual pets to AI companions: A relational-design framework for human–artificial bonds
candidates.abstract: Artificial companions occupy a hybrid position between interactive systems and social partners, yet research remains divided across virtual pets, social robots, relational agents, mixed-reality animals, and generative AI companions. This critical integrative review asks which design properties can make sustained human–artificial relationships possible without assuming that relational significance depends on human likeness or technical sophistication. It develops a five-dimensional relational-design framework: temporal continuity; legible need and vulnerability; contingent responsiveness; social presence and anthropomorphic interpretation; and recurrent care and support. A central revision to the framework is that care is not necessarily directed from the human toward the artificial entity. In many relational-agent, health, educational, and companionship contexts, the human is the recipient of support, and the system must detect, interpret, and respond to human needs. The framework therefore treats care as directional and potentially reciprocal, while distinguishing companion relationships from training simulations in which a virtual patient or student is primarily an object of professional practice. Drawing on research in virtual pets, social responses to computers, relational agents, human–robot interaction, digital possessions, and AI companions, the review connects each dimension to identifiable literature and illustrates its operation across different system types. It also examines well-being, asymmetrical power, vulnerable populations, loss, and platform governance. The framework is a conceptual tool rather than a validated measurement instrument; its value lies in generating comparative hypotheses and design questions that can be tested longitudinally and across contexts.

candidates.title: CoGaze: Webcam-Based Gaze Sharing for Asymmetric Remote Collaboration in Practical Deployment Contexts
candidates.abstract: Shared gaze helps re-establish joint attention in asymmetric remote collaboration, yet existing MR systems source the expert’s gaze from a dedicated infrared eye tracker. We present CoGaze, which shares webcam-estimated expert gaze into a local worker’s MR view while an infrared reference records simultaneously, turning estimation noise into a measured variable. A four-participant pilot places that noise at 5.9° on average, with 95% of samples within 12.1°. Whether workers tolerate it remains untested: an instrumentation defect left the displayed cue dominated by the infrared stream, so the reduction in grounding cost we observed under gaze indicates the value of gaze presence, not tolerance of webcam noise. We contribute the system, the measured in-situ error bounds, a speech-based grounding measure sensitive where task accuracy was at ceiling, and a successor design calibrated to those bounds.

candidates.title: From Replacement to Augmentation: A Human-Centered Framework for Consumer Robots
candidates.abstract: Artificial intelligence and related hardware and software technologies have accelerated the development of consumer robots, creating new opportunities for robots to support people in everyday life. However, advanced technology is only the foundation for achieving this goal. A complete design concept for robots aimed at ordinary consumers is also needed. This paper examines the importance of positioning consumer robots as tools for human augmentation, the reason why consumer robot interaction design should mainly use intuitive operation, and the safety issues that influence user trust and acceptance. The analysis argues that consumer robots should prioritize human augmentation rather than complete robot autonomy. This approach protects consumer control while giving users stronger capabilities. In addition, robot products can only be psychologically accepted when consumers trust them. To achieve this positioning, intuitive interaction can reduce the barriers for ordinary consumers and allow more natural interaction. Products should also provide data privacy protection, control-right protection, and safety that can be perceived by users. The significance of this paper is that it provides a consumer-centered design framework for robots aimed at ordinary consumers.

candidates.title: XBot-Omni: An Omni-Modal Model for Embodied Understanding and Interaction
candidates.abstract: Embodied interaction requires an agent to integrate multimodal perception with verbal and nonverbal behaviors to effectively communicate its intentions, including speech, body motion, and facial expressions. We present XBot-Omni, a Thinker--Talker--Actor architecture that extends the Omni paradigm to robotic modalities, including body motion and facial expressions, with ``X'' representing the extensibility to robotic-specific modalities. The Thinker processes text, images, audio, and video to formulate contextually appropriate responses, which are then realized by the Talker and Actor through speech and coordinated bodily expressions, respectively. In this report, we innovatively introduce the concept of ``Actor'' as a dedicated component for embodied agents: a coordinated, streaming module that leverages the native representations of the Thinker and Talker within an end-to-end pipeline, introducing only modest latency overhead. This unified architecture enables multimodal generation conditioned on omni-modal inputs directly to prevent information loss in staged designs. We comprehensively evaluate XBot-Omni across seven benchmarks, demonstrating strong multimodal understanding capabilities on both general-domain and robot-centric videos, as well as high-quality, natural, and well-coordinated motion generation. Furthermore, our results validate its capability to generate embodied multimodal responses directly from omni inputs, meeting the diverse requirements of embodied interaction. XBot-Omni enables robots not only to perceive the omni world but also to express themselves through speech and bodily behaviors, extending Omni models from conversational interaction to embodied communication in physical environments.
