candidates.title: Dancing with REEM-C: A Robot-To-Human Physical-Social Communication Study
candidates.abstract: Humans often work closely together and relay a wealth of information through physical interaction. Robots, on the other hand, are not yet able to work similarly closely with humans and to effectively convey information when engaging in physical-social human-robot interaction (psHRI). This currently limits the potential of human-robot collaboration to solve real-world problems. This paper investigates how to establish clear and intuitive robot-to-human communication, while considering human comfort during psHRI. We approach this question from the perspective of a leader-follower dancing scenario, in which a full-body humanoid robot leads a human by signaling the next steps through a choice of communication modalities including haptic, visual, and audio signals. This is achieved through the development of a split whole-body control framework combining admittance and impedance control on the upper body, with position control on the lower body for balancing and stepping. Robot-led psHRI participant experiments allowed us to verify controller performance, as well as to build an understanding of what types of communication work better from the perspective of human partners, particularly in terms of perceived effectiveness and comfort.

candidates.title: Robots: Passing by in Public Spaces
candidates.abstract: Robots are increasingly found in public spaces such as sidewalks, parks, and transportation hubs. Delivery robots cross urban streets to transport food and goods; maintenance robots clean public parks; and service robots provide information at museums, train stations and airports. In principle, public spaces are open and accessible to all and are characterized by diverse and plural encounters. As such, robots operating in these environments encounter a wide range of individuals of different ages, physical and mental abilities, and backgrounds. Unlike many forms of social human-robot interaction which presuppose familiarity, shared interests, or repeated engagement, interactions between robots and humans in public spaces are typically brief and incidental and occur without any shared purpose. Despite the growing presence of robots in public environments, existing research lacks a comprehensive conceptualization of human-robot interaction in public spaces and an ethical evaluation of such interaction. This paper makes three main contributions to address this research gap: First, it establishes a framework of “ passing by” human-robot interaction in public spaces, identifying it as a paradigmatic and undertheorized form of encounter between robots and people incidentally co-present with the robot. Second, it argues that passing by interaction can harm passersby when the robot’s behavior is not sufficiently legible to them. Hence, taking the principle of non-maleficence as an ethical baseline, the paper argues that robots operating in public spaces should be designed such that their behavior is intuitively understandable to a sufficient degree. As one possible means of achieving such intuitive understandability, the paper suggests that robots adhere to social rules that humans typically follow when navigating public spaces. However, conforming to these norms also carries the ethical risk of reproducing and reinforcing discriminatory practices, thereby undermining the diversity and openness that are constitutive of public spaces. Third, the paper examines this tension and translates its normative argument into three design ideals intended to guide the ethically responsible design of robots in public spaces.

candidates.title: Children’s Engagement during Cognitive Assessments with Minimal Robot Intervention
candidates.abstract: Standard pediatric cognitive and projective assessments can be monotonous and provoke anxiety. This reduces children's engagement and compliance and diminishes the quality of observable behavior. In this work, we present a workflow that transfers routine paper-and-pencil tasks to a tablet application and adds a NAO humanoid robot as a social partner. Our goal is to provide a robot-and-tablet system for standardized assessments. In this exploratory study, we focused on quantifying the added contribution of the robot to engagement compared to a tablet-only system. To this end, we evaluated the workflow in a pediatric clinic with 24 participants, each with a distinct neurodevelopmental disorder diagnosis, using a controlled, between-subjects design. The tablet-only condition delivered the same activities and pacing without robot cues. This served as a control to isolate the effect of social scaffolding. Licensed therapists rated engagement using the Pediatric Assessment of Rehabilitation Engagement (PARE) scale. Our preliminary findings suggest that the robot's presence supported higher observable engagement and sustained participation without altering the rapport within the child–therapist–robot triad. Moreover, results in the PARE scale were significantly different between the two conditions when considering the age of the little patients (with mean age 10 vs. 8, respectively). While the small sample size and age distribution warrant cautious interpretation, this work highlights a robot's potential contribution to children's engagement during standardized assessment.

candidates.title: Mirror Skin: In Situ Visualization of Robot Touch Intent on Robot Skin
candidates.abstract: Effective communication of robot touch intent is essential for safe and predictable physical human-robot interaction. While intent communication has been widely studied, existing approaches lack the spatial specificity and semantic depth necessary to efficiently convey robot touch intent. We present Mirror Skin, a cephalopod-inspired concept that mirrors in-situ visual representations of a human’s body parts onto the corresponding robot’s touch region to communicate who shall initiate touch, where it will occur, and when it is imminent. We informed the design of Mirror Skin through a structured design exploration with experts and demonstrate the real-world feasibility of Mirror Skin with a proof-of-concept prototype. User studies in VR and with the physical prototype showed that Mirror Skin significantly improves accuracy and response times for interpreting touch intent and improves the user experience during physical human-robot interactions.

candidates.title: When thanks have nowhere to go: emotional indebtedness in the age of service robots
candidates.abstract: Introduction: When hotel service robots deliver meaningful service, customers may experience emotional indebtedness-a moral-emotional state arising from perceived obligation without a clear target for reciprocity. This study examines how social (social presence, enjoyment) and nonsocial (novelty, performance) attributes of service robots influence emotional indebtedness and subsequent brand loyalty. Methods: Survey data were collected from 462 hotel guests in China with direct service robot experience. Structural equation modeling (SEM) with maximum likelihood estimation was employed, incorporating second-order latent constructs and multi-group analysis by anthropomorphism level. Results: Social attributes significantly increased emotional indebtedness, whereas nonsocial attributes either reduced or failed to elicit such responses. Emotional indebtedness positively predicted brand loyalty. Multi-group analyses revealed that the effect of social attributes on emotional indebtedness was invariant across anthropomorphism levels, whereas anthropomorphism moderated the relationship between nonsocial attributes and emotional indebtedness and the conversion of indebtedness into brand loyalty. Discussion: These findings extend social exchange theory to robot-mediated hospitality services, demonstrating that customers' moral-emotional responses depend more on how robot interactions are socially interpreted than on functional performance alone. Anthropomorphism functions as a selective boundary condition rather than a uniform amplifier of emotional engagement.

candidates.title: Ask to Evolve: A Unified Harness for Lifelong Embodied Navigation with Hybrid Action Space and Persistent Memory
candidates.abstract: Giving embodied agents the freedom to act autonomously, initiate interactions, and understand their surroundings through experience is a step toward bringing them to life in the physical world. Realizing this vision requires action, interaction, and memory to work together, so that each encounter can inform current decisions and contribute experience for future tasks. We present EvoLife, a unified navigation harness that enables a multimodal embodied agent to choose how to move, when to ask, and what experience to carry forward. Its hybrid action space supports waypoint navigation, local discrete adjustments, pixel-based navigation, and object-directed navigation. Active interaction allows the agent to seek clarification or assistance when it encounters ambiguity or difficulty, while persistent spatial memory binds observations and dialogue to places, retaining useful experience to guide subsequent visits. We evaluate eight benchmarks across four task families: vision-language navigation, object navigation, interactive instance navigation, and continuous multi-task navigation. With an average of only 1.87 active interactions per episode, our method achieves a first-visit success rate (SR) of 100% across four 100-episode sets spanning vision-language navigation and object navigation. Complete-sequence SR reaches 98% on 50 LHPR-VLN sequences and 94% on 50 GOAT-Bench sequences. In the R2R revisit setting, success weighted by path length (SPL) increases from 82.23% to 93.31% with retained experience. Multi-day physical navigation further demonstrates exploration, proactive help-seeking, and revisiting remembered places. Together, these results advance the vision of bringing embodied agents to life through autonomous action, proactive interaction, and the accumulation and reuse of experience.

candidates.title: Human Centric Embodied Intelligence for Soft Wearable Robotics
candidates.abstract: Soft wearable robots have evolved rapidly from proof‐of‐concept devices into promising platforms for rehabilitation, occupational assistance, and human augmentation. As the field matures, its central challenge extends beyond developing softer materials and more capable actuators to integrating sensing, intelligence, and human adaptation into systems that users can wear comfortably, trust, and benefit from over long periods. This transition motivates the concept of human centric embodied intelligence (HCEI). In HCEI, intelligence emerges from the coupled human–robot system, through the interaction of morphology, multimodal sensing, adaptive cognition, compliant actuation, and the wearer's own physiological and behavioral adaptation. To organize this perspective, we introduce the perception–cognition–actuation–augmentation (PCAA) framework. It proposes that design start from the augmentation objective, the change sought in the wearer's function, and that the requirements on perception, cognition, and actuation be derived from that objective rather than from the actuating mechanism. Using this framework, we review advances in soft materials, wearable sensing, artificial intelligence, actuation, human–robot interaction, digital twins, clinical translation, manufacturing, regulation, and ethics, and trace how these interdependent components together shape long‐term personalization and real‐world deployment. The review aims to guide future research, encourage interdisciplinary collaboration, and speed the translation of soft wearable robots toward personalized, predictive, and human‐centric wearable intelligence.

candidates.title: LEXICAL AND PRAGMATIC FEATURES OF FAN COMMUNICATION ON THE SOCIAL MEDIA PLATFORM X
candidates.abstract: The widespread use of social media has changed the ways in which audiences interact with popular culture, leading to the emergence of online fan communities. An online fandom is examined as a community of people united by a common interest in a particular object of popular culture who actively interact on social media. When fans interact online, they exchange information, express their opinions, emotions, attitudes towards actors, events and other fans, creating a sense of community. Although fan culture has been examined in cultural studies, psychology and media studies, the linguistic organisation of fan communication on social media platforms has received limited scholarly attention. The aim of this article is to study the linguistic characteristics of fandom communication on the X platform (formerly Twitter), with particular attention to its lexical and pragmatic features. The analysis is based on a corpus of posts and comment threads related to popular films, television series and actors. It identifies the main features of fandom communication on social media, including the construction of group identity, the use of linguistic devices to express evaluation and emotion, parasocial relationships between fans and celebrities and the use of intertextual references. The results demonstrate that fandom discourse on X is characterised by lexical innovation, the use of personal pronouns (we, us, our vs. they, them, their) and fandom- specific community labels to establish in-group identity, the frequent use of online slang and evaluative language. Fans reduce the perceived social distance between themselves and celebrities through the use of diminutive forms of address and nicknames. Communication within fandom spaces is also highly intertextual, it relies on shared vocabulary, memes and inside jokes based on common knowledge of films, television series, celebrities and fan culture. This study contributes to current research on online communication and language use on social media platforms.

candidates.title: OpenZilo: An Open Smart-Ring Platform for Human-Centric Sensing and Interaction with Robots
candidates.abstract: Wearable robot interfaces must connect user input to timely physical action. We present the proposed platform, an open smart-ring platform for studying this connection across task stages. The ring integrates a microphone, an inertial measurement unit, photoplethysmography, and skin-temperature sensing. Its software architecture separates acquisition, event interpretation, interaction policy, and robot execution. We characterize seven operating modes and evaluate speech and gesture control with 10 participants. Across five commands and 250 trials per modality, speech and gestures achieved task success rates of 90.4% and 88.8%, respectively. Recognition accuracy exceeded task success for both modalities. Gaussian hidden Markov models achieved higher accuracy than a support vector machine across three vocabulary sizes, with longer scoring times. Following a shared spoken task start, gesture-based adjustments had shorter median response times than speech. Whole-task success was 70.0% with gestures and 64.0% with speech. We further examine physiological-event-triggered robot interaction using simulated event notifications. Mean notification-receipt-to-arrival times were 11.71 s for the robot and 9.20 s for an on-site person. These descriptive findings support evaluating wearable robot interfaces through both recognition and physical outcomes, with timing measures appropriate to each task stage.

candidates.title: A hardware-aware open-source framework for design space exploration of mixed-signal spiking neural networks
candidates.abstract: Introduction Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing at the edge requires simulation tools that can capture the non-ideal behavior of mixed-signal spiking neural network (SNN) hardware while supporting system-level design exploration. Methods This work presents an open-source hardware-aware simulation framework for mixed-signal SNNs that enables comparative analysis across neuron, synapse and architecture choices. The framework supports multiple neuron models, including Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF), Hodgkin-Huxley (HH) and Axon-Hillock (AH), together with non-volatile analog synapses based on floating-gate transistors and ReRAM devices. By incorporating device-level non-linearities directly into PyTorch-based training and inference, the tool enables optimization of physical synaptic parameters rather than idealized abstract weights. Results The framework is evaluated on standard neuromorphic benchmarks, including N-MNIST, DVS Gesture and Spiking Heidelberg Digits (SHD). For each model dataset configuration, it reports classification accuracy together with hardware-oriented metrics such as silicon area, power consumption and quantization sensitivity. In addition, mismatch analysis has been implemented to capture the impact of real silicon fabrication-based effects, such as device-to-device and transistor-level variability, on network behavior. Discussion These capabilities enable cross-layer design space exploration and help identify neuron-synapse configurations that best satisfy application-specific constraints on accuracy, energy efficiency, area and hardware fidelity.

candidates.title: Disaster Robotics in the Deep Learning Era]{Disaster Robotics in the Deep Learning Era: A Systematic Review of Platforms, Autonomy, Methods, Datasets, Challenges, and Future Research Directions
candidates.abstract: Disaster robotics enables responders to sense and act at a disaster site from a safe distance, converting responder risk into an equipment one. The field is increasingly shaped by deep learning and, most recently, by foundation models. However, existing surveys adopt a single perspective or platform class, predate the deep learning era or remain largely narrative. Moreover, none grades every reviewed work on a common validation maturity scale. This paper presents a systematic review of disaster robotics in the deep learning era, restricted to disaster-connected works evaluated on disaster data or in real, replicated or simulated emergency settings. The evolution of the field is traced through successive research phases, from teleoperated platforms to foundation-model interfaces and responder-grounded field autonomy. A multi-criteria taxonomy is formed, covering response tasks, robotic platforms, perception, autonomy, learning strategies, foundation model types, human-robot teaming, coordination, communication and deployment, disaster domains, and validation maturity. Each criterion is analyzed comparatively, with critical insights into the strengths and limitations of its categories under field conditions. Additionally, public datasets and benchmarks are reviewed. Current challenges are also paired with future research directions, from data acquisition and field hardening to verifiable autonomy, responder trust and evaluation. The analysis shows that systems deployed at real incidents still rely predominantly on model-based methods. It also shows that recent research leans increasingly on simulation and benchmark evaluation. Finally, foundation models have entered the field mainly as perception front ends and mission-level planners rather than as embodied policies, without yet reaching a real incident.

candidates.title: From Companion to Guardian: Designing an Emergency Support System Using a Quadruped Robot for Older Adults
candidates.abstract: As older adults increasingly live alone, emergency support becomes an important function for home companion robots. In Australia, demand for the care and support workforce is projected to nearly double between 2020-21 and 2049-50. Service robots such as robot dogs may support older adults by combining everyday companionship with assistance when human support is not immediately available. We present the design and implementation of a domestic companion-robot system on a Unitree Go1 quadruped platform that combines companionship with emergency awareness and response. The system uses a three-stage interaction model consisting of companion, danger-awareness, and emergency modes. A rule-based escalation policy combines signs detected from visual and speech input to determine the current risk level and adjust how long the robot waits for the user to confirm safety before entering emergency mode. Additional detected signs can shorten this waiting time. Users can confirm safety, request immediate help, stop robot motion, or reset the system. We verified the implemented decision rules and escalation timing through 105 automated trials and 25 staged physical trials. Additional visual evidence shortened the waiting time, and the system entered emergency mode when the waiting time ended without confirmation.

candidates.title: Robots as lab partners: chemists’ perspectives for informing the design of robot-assisted experimentation
candidates.abstract: Experimental laboratory work involves repetitive, labour-intensive manual procedures and strict safety protocols, making it an attractive area for Robotics and Artificial Intelligence (RAI). With research currently focused on technical innovation, there has been little work investigating the human factors of chemist-robot collaboration, and how these technologies will change the nature of work in chemistry. Understanding chemists’ requirements and perspectives is vital to the successful deployment and acceptance of RAI in laboratories. We examined the potential for robot-assisted chemistry experimentation through the perspective of future users by conducting contextual inquiries and semi-structured interviews with nine experimental chemists at various career levels with and without laboratory automation experience. Reflexive thematic analysis was used to gain a situated understanding of how their work could benefit from automation, as well as their perspectives and opinions on working alongside robots. We found that our participants are open to robot-assisted experimentation and have clear ideas for human-robot partnerships in the lab. We identified eight themes characterising chemists’ desired applications, the implementation requirements, and the perspectives on the adoption of robot-assisted experimentation. These findings show that successful acceptance of robot-assisted experimentation depends not only on technical innovation, but also on addressing the practical barriers and concerns of the chemists who will work alongside these systems. The key concern being that RAI should not constrain, but rather complement the role of the chemist in knowledge discovery. The findings contribute to a set of initial design considerations covering hardware, software, and interaction design for successful integration of RAI in experimental laboratory work.

candidates.title: Gemini Robotics in Agriculture: Applications, Models, Fruit Industry, and Future Perspectives
candidates.abstract: Agricultural robotics is progressing from task-specific automation toward embodied systems that integrate multimodal perception, language, reasoning, and physical action. This chapter reviews Gemini Robotics and closely related vision-language model (VLM) and vision-language-action (VLA) developments in the context of agriculture, with particular emphasis on fruit production. It first presents a conceptual agricultural architecture linking sensing, cognition, decision and control, actuation, connectivity, power and safety. It then examines emerging evidence from language-guided agricultural navigation, spatial-memory systems, occlusion-aware harvest planning, VLA-based strawberry harvesting, obstacle separation and text-prompted multi-fruit picking. The reviewed studies show growing capability in navigation, semantic reasoning and closed-loop manipulation, but also expose important limitations in agricultural validation, cross-crop generalization, action datasets, real-time computing, safety and commercial readiness. For fruit systems, the principal technical challenges remain occlusion, maturity and accessibility assessment, three-dimensional localization, delicate detachment and adaptation across cultivars, canopies and seasons. The chapter therefore proposes a future pathway centered on multimodal agricultural foundation models, edge VLA inference, soft and tactile manipulation, continual learning, natural-language human-robot collaboration and coordinated UAV-UGV-manipulator systems. The Gemini Robotics provides a promising foundation for moving agricultural robots from isolated perception-action pipelines toward general-purpose embodied intelligence, although extensive field validation is required before broad deployment.

candidates.title: Imagining Shared Experiences With Robots Predicts Greater Expected Social Connection Through Shared Reality
candidates.abstract: Although the integration of social robots into everyday life is still at an early stage, understanding what facilitates social connection with robots has received increasing research attention. The current research examined whether merely imagining shared experiences with robots increases people's expected social connection with robots, the role of expected shared reality as an underlying mechanism, and the influence of social exclusion on expected shared reality. Across three experiments, participants imagined sharing (vs. not sharing) the experience of eating chocolates with a humanoid robot that ostensibly possessed inner states. In Studies 1a and 1b, when participants imagined sharing an experience with the robot, they expected a greater sense of shared reality, and in turn, expected to feel greater social connection with the robot. In Study 2, socially excluded participants expected to experience greater shared reality with the robot than socially included participants. Together, these findings suggest that imagining shared experiences with robots may serve to foster a sense of social connection with robots by increasing expectations of shared reality.

candidates.title: Risks of counter-stereotypical AI when it replaces human contact
candidates.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are often designed with stereotype-consistent social cues-such as feminized voice assistants in service roles or masculine security robots-to increase acceptance and interaction fluency. Yet these same design choices may reinforce the stereotypes they draw on. Recent work, however, proposes a more optimistic possibility: counter-stereotypical AI-for example, a female-coded technical chatbot or male-coded care robot-may reduce prejudice by functioning as synthetic intergroup contact, repeatedly exposing users to agents that serve as proxy members of social groups and challenge familiar stereotypes. We build on this account but argue that its implications depend critically on whether AI supplements or replaces human interaction. When counter-stereotypical AI adds exposure to underrepresented groups, it may challenge stereotypes by broadening the range of people users associate with particular traits or domains. When it substitutes for humans, however, its effects become more ambivalent. We identify three risks of counter-stereotypical AI as replacement: non-integration, when users treat the agent as a designed persona rather than revising beliefs about people; substitution, when synthetic contact displaces the reciprocal and agentic qualities of human contact; and illusion of inclusion, when visible AI representation is mistaken for institutional inclusion. We position replacement by counter-stereotypical AI as a critical boundary condition for theories of synthetic contact and representational AI, and as a key context for future research on prejudice, technology, and social change.

candidates.title: Robotic Security: A Dual-Domain Analysis of Security Robots and Robot Cybersecurity
candidates.abstract: Robotic security operates across two distinct but increasingly converging domains: the deployment of robots as security agents (security robotics) and the protection of robotic systems from cyber-physical attacks (robot cybersecurity). This paper provides a structured examination of both domains. In the first, security robots—including patrol robots, sentry systems, and autonomous surveillance platforms—are analyzed in terms of their applications, capabilities, and the human–robot interaction challenges they pose. In the second, the unique vulnerabilities of robotic systems are examined, including threats to sensors, actuators, communication channels, and the Robot Operating System (ROS) ecosystem, alongside emerging defense mechanisms such as intrusion detection systems and secure-by-design architectures. We complement the review with an empiricalcomponent: a structured survey of N = 48 security-robot deployments, a simulated evaluation of an intrusion-detection pipeline on robotic network traffic collected from a ROS 2 testbed, and asecondary analysis of published human–robot trust data. Results indicate that (i) fewer than one infive deployed security robots incorporate any documented cyber-hardening, and hardening isstatistically decoupled from network exposure; (ii) a univariate-feature-selection IDS retains 99.3% of baseline macro-F1 while reducing feature dimensionality by 74.4% and halving edge inference latency; and (iii) perceived trust in a security robot is predicted more strongly by perceived integrity than by perceived ability. The paper argues that the increasing autonomy and connectivity ofsecurity robots creates a recursive vulnerability: the very systems deployed to provide securitybecome attractive targets for adversarial compromise. A unified perspective that treats roboticsecurity as a cyber-physical problem—rather than two separate fields—is necessary for the safe and trustworthy deployment of security robotics.

candidates.title: NeuroEvolution of dynamic neural field architectures for Human–Robot joint action
candidates.abstract: Achieving adaptive Human–Robot Interaction (HRI) demands control architectures that generate behaviour through continuous sensorimotor dynamics. Dynamic Neural Fields (DNFs) offer a biologically inspired framework for modelling perception, memory, and action selection, yet designing functional neural-field controllers remains largely manual, limiting their scalability and broader adoption in robotic systems. Here, we introduce an approach for the automated synthesis of the architecture and dynamics of DNF controllers capable of generating normative joint-action behaviours. It builds on NEAT-DNFs, an extension of NeuroEvolution of Augmenting Topologies (NEAT) to neural-field architectures. From a perceptual–motor interface and a specification of the desired behaviour, the approach evolves both intrinsic field dynamics and architectural topology through mutation, crossover, and speciation. We evaluate it in a collaborative packaging task designed to isolate three basic coordination behaviours (complementary action selection, cooperative assistance, and action inhibition) and whose minimal controller can be derived analytically, providing a ground-truth reference for assessing evolved solutions. Across 100 independent runs, the approach discovered viable controllers in 97 cases. Ablation results show that structural growth, minimal initialisation, speciation, and crossover each contribute to performance, with the removal of any one component reducing the success rate, slowing convergence, or producing larger structures. The evolved architectures were topologically minimal, with interpretable activation dynamics grounded in known Dynamic Field Theory (DFT) mechanisms. The highest-performing minimal controller was deployed directly to a physical robot without parameter retuning, generalising to object arrangements beyond those used during evolution. Evolution converged most often on the minimal architecture without any specification of intermediate structure, indicating that behavioural requirements can drive the emergence of the internal processing structure the task requires. These findings demonstrate that functional DNF architectures for joint action can be evolved rather than hand-designed, shifting the designer’s contribution from specifying mechanism to specifying behaviour.

candidates.title: When robots malfunction: children’s and teachers’ responses in Korean preschool classrooms
candidates.abstract: This study investigates how children and teachers in Korean preschool classrooms respond to naturally occurring robot malfunctions during interactions with AI-powered humanoid robots. Over a three-month period, two robots were integrated into naturalistic play sessions with five-year-old children. Drawing on lag-1 sequential analysis, the study identified immediate interactional patterns surrounding robot breakdown episodes. Children’s verbal and embodied reactions – such as repetition, adjusted phrasing, name-calling, emotional disengagement, and laughter – suggest that children actively attempted to manage or restore interaction during robot malfunction episodes. These responses indicate that children treated robots as responsive social actors and adjusted their interactional behaviors during breakdown situations. Robot malfunctions also often involved peers and teachers in managing breakdown situations, turning individual breakdown episodes into socially shared interactional events rather than isolated technical failures. The findings highlight how robot malfunctions become embedded within classroom interactional dynamics. This study contributes to research on classroom-based human–robot interaction by examining the ecological and sequential organization of robot breakdown episodes in naturalistic preschool settings.

candidates.title: Avatar Style and Interpersonal Distance in VR: A Preliminary Multi-modal Study
candidates.abstract: Avatar appearance is a central design choice in social VR, yet its influence on user proxemics and physiological arousal remains unclear. We present a preliminary study examining behavioural, physiological, and self-reported responses during VR encounters with two avatars that differed in kawaii appearance. In a personal space experiment, participants (N = 21) approached a non-kawaii and then a kawaii avatar, presented in a fixed order, while we measured heart rate variability (HRV) and self-selected stopping distance. Contrary to the expectation that cute aesthetics would reduce interpersonal distance, participants maintained significantly greater distance from the kawaii avatar. Physiologically, parasympathetic withdrawal was attenuated in the kawaii condition (smaller decrease in pNN50), while heart rate showed no condition difference. Behavioural stopping distance was not significantly correlated with pNN50 changes, although the study could only detect strong correlations, and self-reported comfort did not fully mirror physiological trends. Because the avatars also differed in height, gender presentation, clothing, and visual extent, these differences cannot be attributed to kawaii appearance alone. Rather than indicating a unified response, the results suggest that avatar style can elicit distinct behavioural and autonomic reactions, underscoring multi-modal evaluation in social VR avatar design.

candidates.title: Synchrony, Affect, and Perceived Autonomy in Virtual Robot-Facilitated Anxiety Support Groups
candidates.abstract: Socially assistive robots could expand access to group-based mental health support when skilled human facilitators are unavailable. However, their effectiveness will depend on whether they foster productive interactions among participants. We examined dyadic head-movement synchrony among 96 participants across 18 virtual robot-facilitated anxiety support group sessions. A human-controlled virtual robot, via a Wizard-of-Oz (WoZ) system, facilitated all sessions. We found that stronger peak synchrony predicted lower post-session negative affect. In contrast, speakers who more often followed listeners' movements reported higher negative affect and state anxiety, demonstrating that synchrony strength and direction capture distinct interpersonal processes. Participants who believed the robot was autonomous showed more genuine synchrony and stronger peaks than those who believed it was human-operated; more negative attitudes toward robots also predicted greater synchrony. These findings support synchrony as an objective, behaviorally grounded measure for evaluating robot-facilitated groups and a potential signal for guiding future autonomous facilitators.

candidates.title: Visual Biomimetics and Foraging Status Shape Honeybee Responses to Robotic Agents
candidates.abstract: Animal–Robot Interaction (ARI) provides a controlled framework for investigating animal behavior and developing socially interactive robots. A key challenge is determining which biologically inspired features enable artificial agents to influence animal decisions and how such effects depend on behavioral state. Here, these questions are investigated in the Italian honeybee (Apis mellifera ligustica). An ARI platform was developed including robotic agents with three levels of visual biomimetic realism: full biomimetic agents (FBAs), partial biomimetic agents (PBAs), and Nonbiomimetic agents (NBAs). Their ability to induce local enhancement, defined as increased selection of an associated food source, was tested in two‐choice assays with newly emerged, foraging‐naïve workers and experienced foragers. Food‐source selection, choice latency, and time to feeding were quantified, with confined living honeybees serving as a biological reference. Experienced foragers preferentially selected food sources associated with FBAs and living honeybees, whereas PBAs and NBAs did not induce significant preferences. Newly emerged workers showed no significant preference for any agent category or living honeybees, although agent configuration influenced temporal aspects of behavior. These findings demonstrate that responses to visual robotic agents depend on foraging status and highlight the importance of behavioral maturation and sensory context when designing socially interactive and adaptive robots.

candidates.title: Benchmarking robots for everyday environments: from lab experiments to real-world operations
candidates.abstract: This study presents an interdisciplinary process for benchmarking service robots in public everyday environments, addressing the gap between laboratory metrics and real-world operation at technology readiness levels 6–7. Three robots were evaluated in three use cases: outdoor park cleaning, pedestrian underpass cleaning, and interactive assistance in a public library. Over three years (2023–2025), seven benchmarking events (a consensus workshop and six on-site evaluations, two per use case) assessed the robots in increasingly realistic settings, from controlled conditions to public operation. An interdisciplinary panel of experts in robotics, human–robot interaction, safety, and economic viability consolidated use-case-specific metrics into a shared evaluation concept refined across three phases. Rather than ranking the robots, the evaluation examined how task fulfillment, interaction quality, safety, and economic viability interact in the transition from laboratory prototype to operational system. Direct quantitative comparability across the heterogeneous use cases remained limited, characteristic of benchmarking at this maturity level. The process yielded cross-case insights: increasing environmental realism introduces challenges that uniform metrics capture only in part; the interaction-quality guideline works best as a modular instrument adapted to each use case; safety was assessed by occupational-safety and product-certification experts who adapted industrial test procedures for public settings; and economic viability proved a cross-cutting dimension. We conclude that benchmarking at higher technology readiness levels is well served by a shared procedure for selecting and documenting metrics across these four categories, with safety as mandatory, rather than by a fixed set of metrics: generalizability lies in the procedure rather than in identical metrics.

candidates.title: OpenDrive: An Open-Source Microdrive for Large-Scale Neurophysiology
candidates.abstract: Neuropixels-NHP probes have ushered in a new era of high-density neurophysiology recording in large animal models. Here, we present OpenDrive, an open-source microdrive system designed specifically for acute insertion of Neuropixels-NHPs. OpenDrive combines a custom motorized microdrive, six-drive control console, and software platform. Compared with commercially available options, OpenDrive offers (1) low cost, (2) precise, accurate, and stable probe movement, (3) scalability to many-probe recording, and (4) open-source hardware designs and software. In our experiments, OpenDrive has already supported recordings from thousands of neurons across a variety of cortical and subcortical structures. By lowering technical barriers and enabling community-driven development with OpenDrive, we aim to accelerate Neuropixels recording in large animal models.

candidates.title: Unveiling the role of virtual streamer’s interaction attributes in shaping consumer-generated value behaviors
candidates.abstract: The interaction attributes of virtual streamers are crucial to their success. This study deconstructs virtual streamers' interaction into two dimensions: interaction intelligence and interaction humanness. Drawing on immersion theory and parasocial relationship theory, the study examines how these interaction attributes are associated with consumer-generated value behaviors, including social media engagement, donation, and purchase intention. Using data from a survey of 479 respondents and structural equation modeling, the results reveal that both the interaction intelligence and interaction humanness of virtual streamers are positively associated with consumer immersion, which, in turn, is positively related to parasocial relationships with virtual streamers. Immersion and parasocial relationships are further associated with social media engagement, donation, and purchase intention. This study advances the theoretical understanding of virtual streamer interaction and provides practical insights for content creators and platforms aiming to foster consumer-generated value behaviors in virtual streaming.

candidates.title: Exploring AI Robot Mobility in Real Residential Environments for People Living with Frailty: An Observational Study
candidates.abstract: As policies increasingly promote assistive robots to support aging in place, little is known about whether real, lived-in homes can accommodate meaningful human–robot cohabitation for people living with frailty. This observational study examined how residential built environments shape such feasibility. Eight assisted-living residences in England (seven single-occupancy and one shared by a couple) were 3D scanned and reconstructed as CAD floor plans to simulate the movement of a commercially available humanoid robot (Pepper). Robot movement was fragmented in all residences because frailty-supporting adaptations, door widths, corridor constraints, and room geometry conflicted with robot clearance and sensing requirements. Critically, high-risk rooms were least accessible: no bedroom allowed full bed access (0/11), and bathrooms were inaccessible in 38% of residences, revealing a dual-user housing and robotics design challenge.

candidates.title: Dynamic identification and control issues for collaborative robots: the KUKA lightweight robot LWR 4+ case
candidates.abstract: Accurate dynamic models are essential for high-performance control, both for trajectory tracking and physical human–robot interaction involving collision detection, reaction, and force control. This work presents a comprehensive framework for dynamic modeling and identification of the KUKA LWR 4+ collaborative robot based on two complementary approaches. The first exploits signals provided by the KUKA Fast Research Interface, combined with nonlinear joint-friction identification to improve torque prediction. The second is a general methodology applicable to collaborative robots with or without joint elasticity. We present the first complete identification and experimental validation of the KUKA LWR 4+ dynamic model using our Penalty-Based Parameter Retrieval framework, demonstrating its ability to retrieve a physically consistent model for a collaborative robot with elastic joints. For the first time for this robot, the approach yields a complete physically consistent set of dynamic parameters suitable for Newton–Euler algorithms, simulation, and internal wrench estimation. The resulting model is compared with the KUKA LWR 4+ model available in CoppeliaSim, which relies on empirically estimated CAD-based parameters. A procedure is also proposed to incorporate an unknown payload without complete re-identification. Although the resulting model accurately captures the robot dynamics, its direct use in torque control requires accounting for the low-level torque loop, which only partially compensates for joint elasticity. A novel recursive least-squares algorithm is therefore proposed to compensate for this effect. Finally, the validated model is employed in sensorless collision detection, isolation, and reaction experiments, demonstrating its suitability for real-time interaction control.

candidates.title: Anthropomorphism in service robots and consumer acceptance: investigating the relationship via a systematic literature review
candidates.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this study is to investigate the effect of social robots anthropomorphism on consumers’ attitudes, acceptance and intention to use social robots. Design/methodology/approach A systematic literature review was conducted to a total of 96 articles that were selected from reputable scientific journals according to the Chartered Association of Business Schools (CABS) Journal Guide, published between 2015 and 2025. The TCCM (Theory-Content-Characteristic-Methodology) framework was used for data analysis, while a systematic content analysis was also performed. Findings The findings of the application of the TCCM framework highlight the most frequently used theories, research development frameworks, methodologies followed and research outcomes. In addition, it draws attention to the factors that act as moderators and mediators in the relationship between the anthropomorphism of social robots and the attitude, acceptance and intention to use them. Finally, the study concludes with recommendations for further research. Originality/value No literature review has examined all related literature on anthropomorphism attitude, acceptance and intention to use social robots.

candidates.title: AffAdapt: AFFect-driven ADAPTive AI Personas for Seamless Conversations
candidates.abstract: AI-generated personas are being increasingly used for support, training and simulations. While generative AI models possess abilities to generate affect-aware responses, their embodiment into visual personas is an active area of investigation. Naturalistic exchanges require understanding of the conversational partners’ turn completions, whether the agent should respond or keep listening and rely on non-verbal cues aligned with one’s emotional states. Seamless human-AI conversation in a multimodal setting requires all modalities being generated to act in coordination. We present AffAdapt, a seamless interaction design framework for AI-personas, which coordinates streaming speech recognition, proactive turn-management, persona-grounded response generation, a persistent emotional state, and synchronized embodied output into a single interaction loop. We demonstrate the architecture in the context of practicing sensitive, high-stakes conversations, and report an initial case study showing fluid turn management and adaptive, persona-consistent behavior, alongside open challenges in interruption handling, open-ended dialogue, and multimodal affective alignment. AffAdapt’s interaction loop is a generalizable pattern for coordinating timing, identity, and affect in real-time AI personas - applicable to training, coaching, education, and simulation contexts wherever believable, responsive interaction matters.

candidates.title: Let Me Look at You: Advanced Facial Expression Modeling for Conversational Speech Synthesis
candidates.abstract: Conversational Speech Synthesis (CSS) is a fundamental component of human-computer interaction, aiming to generate contextually appropriate, expressive, and empathetic speech. However, facial expressions encode subtle and rich affective cues that are crucial for empathetic speech interaction, whereas existing approaches often overlook this important modality. In addition, the lack of large-scale natural conversational datasets with both speech and visual modalities also limits the development of visual affect understanding in conversational settings. To address these limitations, we propose FacialTalker, a facial-expression-aware CSS framework built upon a large language model backbone. To efficiently encode facial expressions, we propose AUTokenizer, a single-codebook visual tokenizer that discretizes each frame-level facial expression into a compact token, trained with supervision from combinations of facial Action Units. We further introduce a dual direct preference optimization (DualDPO) strategy, which extends the DPO by jointly imposing preference constraints on both visual and speech token sequences, to enhance the model's understanding of facial expressions and speech semantics in multimodal conversational contexts. Moreover, we construct VSDD-1K, a large-scale multimodal dialogue dataset collected through a fully automated pipeline from real-world Internet conversations, comprising over 1,033 hours of synchronized speaker videos and speech, with more than 85% of frames containing valid faces. Extensive objective and subjective experiments demonstrate that FacialTalker consistently outperforms strong baselines in facial-expression perception and speech synthesis quality, generating speech that is more natural, expressive, and better aligned with the conversational context. The results also validate the effectiveness of our training strategy and dataset construction pipeline. The project page: https://github.com/walker-hyf/FacialTalker.

candidates.title: EmoBench-M: Benchmarking Emotional Intelligence for Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: With the integration of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) into robotic systems and AI applications, embedding emotional intelligence (EI) capabilities is essential for enabling these models to perceive, interpret, and respond to human emotions effectively in real-world scenarios. Existing static, text-based, or text-image benchmarks overlook the multimodal complexities of real interactions and fail to capture the dynamic, context-dependent nature of emotional expressions, rendering them inadequate for evaluating MLLMs' EI capabilities. To address these limitations, we introduce EmoBench-M, a systematic benchmark grounded in established psychological theories, designed to evaluate MLLMs across 13 evaluation scenarios spanning three hierarchical dimensions: foundational emotion recognition (FER), conversational emotion understanding (CEU), and socially complex emotion analysis (SCEA). Evaluation was conducted on 27 state-of-the-art MLLMs, using both objective task-specific metrics and LLM-based evaluation, revealing a substantial performance gap relative to human-level competence. Even the best-performing models, Gemini-3.0-Pro and GPT-5.2, achieve the highest scores on EmoBench-M, 70.5 and 66.5 points. Specialized models such as AffectGPT exhibit uneven performance across EmoBench-M, demonstrating strengths in certain scenarios but generally lacking comprehensive emotional intelligence. By providing a comprehensive, multimodal evaluation framework, EmoBench-M captures both the strengths and weaknesses of current MLLMs across diverse emotional contexts. All benchmark resources, including datasets and code, are publicly available at Emobench-M , facilitating further research and advancement in MLLM emotional intelligence.

candidates.title: ImaGGen: Zero-Shot Generation of Co-Speech Semantic Gestures Grounded in Language and Image Input
candidates.abstract: Human communication combines speech with expressive nonverbal cues such as hand gestures that serve manifold communicative functions. Yet, current generative AI-based gesture generation approaches are, for the most part, restricted to simple, repetitive beat gestures that accompany the rhythm of speaking but do not contribute to communicating semantic meaning. This article tackles a core challenge in co-speech gesture synthesis: generating iconic or deictic gestures that are semantically coherent with a verbal utterance. Our basic assumption is that such gestures cannot be derived from language input alone, which inherently lacks the visual meaning that is often carried autonomously by gestures. We therefore introduce a zero-shot system that generates gestures from a given language input and is additionally informed by imagistic input, without manual annotation or human intervention. Our method integrates an image analysis pipeline that extracts key object properties such as shape, symmetry, and alignment, together with a semantic matching module that links these visual details to spoken text. An inverse kinematics engine then synthesizes iconic and deictic gestures and combines them with co-generated natural beat gestures for coherent multimodal communication. A comprehensive user study demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach. In scenarios where speech alone was ambiguous, gestures generated by our system significantly improved participants’ ability to identify object properties, confirming their interpretability and communicative value. While challenges remain in representing complex shapes, our results highlight the importance of context-aware semantic gestures for creating expressive and collaborative virtual agents or avatars, marking a substantial step forward towards efficient and robust, embodied human-agent interaction. More information and example videos are available here: https://hvoss-tech.github.io/ImaGGen/.

candidates.title: Can privacy and security concerns coexist with device adoption? Internet privacy and security concerns and smart eldercare device adoption among older adults
candidates.abstract: Privacy and information security concerns are widely viewed as barriers to older adults’ adoption of smart eldercare devices, yet much of the existing evidence is based on adoption intentions or single-device settings. Using data from the 2023 China Longitudinal Aging Social Survey (CLASS), this study examines adults aged 65 and above and uses survey-weighted Probit models and average marginal effects to assess the relationship between general Internet privacy and information security concerns and smart elderly care device adoption. The results show that Internet privacy and information security concerns are positively associated with smart eldercare device adoption. This positive association is observed for both low-information-exposure health self-monitoring devices and high-information-exposure smart eldercare devices. The positive association between Internet privacy and information security concerns and the adoption of high-information-exposure smart eldercare devices is stronger at higher levels of digital competence. Among older adults with such concerns, greater healthcare needs and family digital support are also positively associated with adoption of high-information-exposure smart eldercare devices. These findings suggest that general Internet privacy and information security concerns can coexist with smart eldercare device adoption and may also be observed alongside greater digital exposure among older adults. The study extends privacy calculus theory in the context of older adults’ digital technology use and provides evidence for more targeted risk communication, differentiated privacy protection, and digital support for older adults.

candidates.title: Souffleur: A Glanceable Display for Mobile Voice Conversations
candidates.abstract: The speech capabilities of mobile devices have grown, but their displays still rely on a text-based chat. When resuming a voice chat after a context switch, the last messages may not convey the key points of the conversation. Autobiographical use and sessions with external participants led to design goals for a mobile-first, speech-driven, glanceable display that helps users continue their reasoning from where they left off. We implement these goals in Souffleur and evaluate it in a between-subjects study with 48 participants. Compared with a conventional chat transcript, we found no reliable difference in how easily participants followed and resumed short voice conversations, nor in effort, attention or recall, although Souffleur reduces the conversation to a few short phrases.

candidates.title: User-Informed Design of a Psychological Support Social Pet Robot for Community-Dwelling People With Long-Term Physical Disabilities: A Formative Study
candidates.abstract: Background Community-dwelling people with long-term physical disabilities may experience pain that interferes with daily and social activities and is associated with poorer mental wellbeing. A home-based psychological support social pet robot could offer mood check-ins, companionship, supportive interaction, and mindfulness guidance for community-dwelling people with long-term physical disabilities. Preliminary evidence is needed to understand their preferences and translate them into candidate design requirements. Objective This study aimed to identify preliminary needs and preferences to inform a psychological support social pet robot for community-dwelling people with long-term physical disabilities, offering mood check-ins, companionship, and mindfulness guidance at home. Methods We conducted a 3-phase formative user-informed design study comprising initial concept development, qualitative target user interviews, and a design workshop. Six community-dwelling adults with long-term physical disabilities took part in the interviews, and one participant also answered the workshop questions by telephone. Four authors used modified workshop materials to synthesize the interview findings and separate responses into an early product plan. Results Qualitative content analysis of the interview transcripts produced 5 themes. These were emotional support, soft touch and appearance, mindfulness delivery, context of use, and ease of use and accessibility. Participants expressed preferences about companionship, touch, use settings, and interaction effort. The author workshop combined these findings with author and technical judgments to develop candidate requirements for dialogue and mindfulness delivery. The resulting psychological support concept combined mood check-ins and companion-oriented interaction with flexible mindfulness guidance. The design also needed to consider pain and daily routines. After the workshop, the authors developed a physical proof-of-concept prototype. It implemented only part of the candidate requirements and included additional author or technical choices. Conclusions For this small community-dwelling sample, target user input showed that home use, physical access, companionship, and flexible support were important. Mindfulness was one component of the broader psychological support role, alongside mood check-ins and optional companion interaction. The prototype illustrates but does not validate the early requirements. Further studies should include people with a wider range of long-term physical disabilities and test usability, accessibility, privacy, and nursing value.

candidates.title: SentiAvatar: Towards Expressive and Interactive Digital Humans
candidates.abstract: We present SentiAvatar, a framework for building expressive interactive 3D digital humans, and use it to create SuSu, a virtual character that speaks, gestures, and emotes in real time. Achieving such a system remains challenging, as it requires jointly addressing three key problems: the lack of large-scale high-quality multimodal data, robust semantic-to-motion mapping, and fine-grained frame-level motion-prosody synchronization. To solve these problems, first, we build SuSuInterActs (21K clips, 37 hours), a dialogue corpus captured via optical motion capture around a single character with synchronized speech, full-body motion, and facial expressions. Second, we pre-train a Motion Foundation Model on 200K+ motion sequences, equipping it with rich action priors that go well beyond the conversation. We then propose an audio-aware plan-then-infill architecture that decouples sentence-level semantic planning from frame-level prosody-driven interpolation, so that generated motions are both semantically appropriate and rhythmically aligned with speech. Experiments show that SentiAvatar achieves state-of-the-art on both SuSuInterActs (R@1 43.64%, nearly 2× the best baseline) and BEATv2 (FGD 4.941, BC 8.078), producing 6\,s of output in 0.3s with unlimited multi-turn streaming.

candidates.title: Do We Really Need Multimodal Emotion Language Models Larger Than 1B Parameters?
candidates.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have significantly improved the performance of multimodal emotion recognition (MER) and enabled interpretable description generation by jointly modeling video, audio, and language, etc. However, these performance improvements are often accompanied by an increase in model parameter size (e.g, at least 7B), which simultaneously incurs high computational costs and reduces inference efficiency, thereby hindering real-time deployment on resource-constrained platforms such as robots and mobile devices. This raises a fundamental question: do we really need the multimodal MER model larger than 1B parameters for high-quality MER? In this paper, we challenge the assumption that larger models are inherently necessary and proposes a lightweight MER framework (called Light-MER ), which achieves better and faster multimodal sentiment understanding and recognition through knowledge distillation. It can transfer knowledge from a strong, large-scale teacher model to a lightweight sub-billion-parameter student model, aiming to preserve rich multimodal emotion reasoning and recognition while substantially improving deployment efficiency. Specifically, we introduce two new optimization strategies to enhance knowledge transfer: (1) a new optimal transport loss that combines Sliced Wasserstein Distance with hidden-state alignment, and (2) a new multi-reward optimization strategy based on GRPO that balances MER performance and efficiency, aimed at further enhancing the learning capabilities of student models. Extensive experiments on nine benchmark datasets demonstrate that Light-MER achieves state-of-the-art performance while significantly improving inference efficiency. This highlights the strong potential of small multimodal emotion language models for future research. Code is available at https://github.com/GAIR-Lab/Light-MER.

candidates.title: Trust formation across AI embodiments: how robotic, virtual, and embedded systems shape user behavior in healthcare
candidates.abstract: Purpose Trust in artificial intelligence (AI) systems shapes user behavior and technology acceptance, yet limited research compares how different AI embodiments influence trust formation. This study aims to examine how robotic, virtual, and embedded AI affect cognitive trust in healthcare contexts. Design/methodology/approach An experimental study was conducted to assess the effects of tangibility, transparency, reliability, task characteristics, and immediacy behaviors on cognitive trust across three AI embodiments. Participants evaluated healthcare scenarios involving robotic, virtual or embedded AI systems, and trust-related perceptions were analyzed across conditions. Findings Significant perceptual differences emerged across AI embodiments. Virtual AI was perceived as less tangible than robotic and embedded AI, while embedded AI was rated highest in technical intelligence but lowest in social intelligence. Despite these differences, overall cognitive trust did not significantly vary across embodiments. However, the mechanisms of trust formation were embodiment-specific. Reliability consistently predicted trust across all conditions. Transparency and immediacy behaviors enhanced trust in robotic AI, tangibility and social intelligence drove trust in virtual AI, and immediacy behaviors were especially critical for embedded AI. Originality/value This study advances AI trust research by positioning embodiment as a boundary condition that shapes mechanisms of trust formation rather than overall trust levels. It extends prior work by demonstrating that trust antecedents operate differently across AI forms and by embedding this analysis within healthcare, where risk and task sensitivity fundamentally influence trust dynamics.

candidates.title: Exploring Emotional Attachment to Artificial Intelligence Companions: A Cross-Cultural Qualitative Study of Psychological Needs, Loneliness, and Human–AI Relationships in Pakistan and the United States
candidates.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) companions has introduced new forms of human–technology interaction in which individuals increasingly experience emotional connection, psychological support, and companionship through digital systems. This study explores emotional attachment to AI companions by examining the psychological needs, loneliness experiences, and human–AI relationship patterns of users in Pakistan and the United States. Using a qualitative interpretive research design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 20 AI companion users, including 10 participants from each cultural context. Data were analyzed through reflexive thematic analysis, resulting in five major themes: AI as an emotionally safe space, loneliness and unmet psychological needs, consistency and attachment formation, negotiation of authenticity, and dependency risks. Drawing upon Attachment Theory and Self-Determination Theory, the findings demonstrate that AI companions may provide meaningful emotional utility by fulfilling needs for connection, validation, and psychological comfort, while remaining distinct from human relationships. The study contributes an integrated AI Attachment–Need Fulfillment perspective and highlights the importance of responsible AI design, ethical guidelines, and balanced human–AI interaction.

candidates.title: Semantic-Enhanced Sparse Temporal Modeling for Dynamic Engagement Estimation in Multimodal Interactions
candidates.abstract: Dynamic engagement estimation aims to infer participants' evolving engagement states from continuous multimodal interaction streams. Existing approaches typically combine acoustic, pose, and visual representations with temporal models to capture observable interaction patterns. However, conversational semantics are difficult to align with frame-level engagement annotations in the same manner as continuous audio-visual signals, leaving dialogue context less effectively exploited in existing temporal modeling pipelines. Moreover, engagement annotations often evolve smoothly over time, making dense frame-level modeling computationally redundant and potentially sensitive to local annotation noise. To address these issues, we propose SEST, a Semantically-Enhanced Sparse Temporal framework that models engagement-related information from both semantic and temporal perspectives. SEST leverages Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to extract multimodal semantic embeddings, providing dialogue-aware contextual information beyond conventional frame-level features. In parallel, SEST replaces dense-to-dense temporal modeling with a sparse-to-dense pathway, where continuous frame sequences are first encoded into compact temporal dynamics to reduce redundant computation and broaden temporal coverage, then fused with semantic context and recovered to the original label resolution for dense engagement prediction. Experiments on the MultiMediate'26 Multi-domain Engagement Estimation (MEE2026) benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness of SEST, which achieved first place in the challenge. Code is available at https://github.com/MSA-LMC/SEST.

candidates.title: Great Listeners, Poor Decision-Makers: Rethinking Agentic Audio AI
candidates.abstract: Audio artificial intelligence (AI) now recognizes speech, sounds, and music remarkably well, yet voice agents still act when they should not: they execute commands addressed to others, act on misheard content, and commit before the user finishes speaking. This position article argues that the bottleneck in agentic audio AI has shifted from recognition to decision-making. We propose a reference architecture with an explicit decision layer, separate from perception and reasoning, that chooses whether to act, wait, ask, or remain silent from evidence on addressedness, speaker identity, content confidence, tool reliability, utterance completeness, and action risk. We motivate the design through six recurring decision failures and a decision-theoretic argument that transcript confidence alone is insufficient to justify an action. We implement the layer with fuzzy inference, evolutionary optimization, and sequential decision-making, and evaluate it through simulations, ablations, and recorded audio, including egocentric recordings. Addressedness and speaker evidence matter most, risk-aware gating suppresses costly errors, and well-tuned policies perform similarly, with fuzzy gates more robust to overconfident addressedness estimates. On recorded audio, explicit gating cuts executed side talk from 41\% to 7--10\% while serving 83--85\% of valid requests under successful clarification, outperforming prompting-based baselines. These results support explicit action gating as an architectural requirement for reliable voice agents.

candidates.title: FEND: Far-End Detection in Outbound Voice AI Calls
candidates.abstract: When a conversational Voice AI agent places an outbound call, the far end may be a live person, a voicemail greeting, an interactive voice response (IVR) system, or increasingly another AI system answering on the callee's behalf. Standard Answering Machine Detection (AMD) reports only whether a human or a machine picked up, a design meant for human call centres, where one machine is as uninteresting as another. That single bit does not tell a Voice AI agent what to do, since leaving a voicemail message, navigating an IVR and holding a short exchange with another AI are three different actions and a two-valued label cannot distinguish them. In 1,000 randomly sampled calls from our own outbound deployment, a live person answered 48.1%, a voicemail system 44.6%, an AI 6.9% and an IVR 0.4%. Our proposed framework, FEND, reads the far end's audio and its streaming transcript and runs one detector for each automated class (voicemail, IVR, AI callee), with human the default when nothing fires, returning a single label within 20 seconds. On a public benchmark the voicemail components reach 100% accuracy without ever misclassifying a live human, where Asterisk's AMD misclassifies 30 to 66% of them. For the AI callee, acoustic features do not transfer across recording conditions, but speech timing does, separating AI from human at 0.952 ROC-AUC, because synthesised speech leaves far shorter gaps between words. On production traffic, separating a live person from any automated far end reaches F1 0.979, and only 2.9% of live people are given an automated label, the error that matters most for an agent acting on the result.

candidates.title: A Segmented Framework for Cryptocurrency Adoption
candidates.abstract: Existing research often treats cryptocurrency adoption as uniform, overlooking differences among assets and users. This article develops a typology linking adopter profiles to institutional orientation, financial capability, technological embeddedness, and asset affinity. The article develops a conceptual typology through taxonomy-development logic, anchored in behavioral-institutional orientation: how individuals engage with cryptocurrency as a financial and socio-technical alternative. The typology identifies three ideal types: long-term investors, linked to bitcoin as a portfolio asset; resilient crypto traders, linked to stablecoins for monetary protection and resilience; and crypto-natives, linked to Ethereum/DeFi for participation, autonomy, and experimentation. The article moves beyond monolithic technology-adoption models and deconstructs the “cryptocurrency user” as uniform. It shifts focus from trust in technology to trust in the financial status quo, highlighting institutional distrust and inflation as segment-specific drivers.

candidates.title: Exploring Non-Verbal Robot Character Emotion through Kinesics: A Case Study of the Animated Film WALL-E
candidates.abstract: Non-verbal communication is central to animated storytelling, particularly in films that rely on minimal dialogue. Previous studies of non-verbal communication in animation have focused largely on human and animal characters, leaving robot characters, whose mechanical bodies lack many human features, comparatively unexamined. This study investigates how non-verbal robot characters express emotion through body language, using the Pixar animated feature film WALL-E (2008) as a case study. Adopting a qualitative design, the study first reviewed twelve previous studies of non-verbal communication in animation to identify the dominant elements of analysis, and found that kinesics was applied in all twelve. Selected scenes featuring the robot characters WALL-E and EVE were then analysed using Birdwhistell’s Kinesics Theory, supported by the Facial Action Coding System (FACS), across three kinesic elements: facial expression, gesture, and posture. The findings show that both characters convey five basic emotions (surprise, fear, joy, sadness, and anger) through stylised eye shapes, mechanical “eyebrows”, hand and arm gestures, movement speed, and whole-body posture. Their mechanical design does not prevent emotional expression; instead, human emotional cues are translated into forms suited to each character’s design. The study extends kinesics-based research in animation to robot characters and offers practical insight for animators and character designers. Future studies should examine additional non-verbal elements and more complex emotions.
